scenarios.scenarioText: Skyline Aviation Ltd is a listed airline whose Board has 9 directors, of whom 4 are independent directors. Its Chairperson, Mr. Banerjee, is also the Managing Director (an executive chairperson). Capt. Mehra, a retired pilot, is proposed for appointment to Skyline's Board; he already holds 18 directorships, of which 9 are in public companies. Skyline has not filed its financial statements or annual returns for FY 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 (three consecutive years). One sitting director, Mr. Sethi, was convicted of an offence four months ago and sentenced to 7 months' imprisonment. A Board meeting was convened on only 3 days' notice to approve a fresh ₹120 crore borrowing; of the 9 directors, 3 are personally interested in that borrowing.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · Nov 2023] Skyline's Board has 9 directors and 4 independent directors. Given that its Chairperson is also the Managing Director, is the Board's composition compliant with the independent-director requirement?

options.A: No — because the Chairperson is an executive (and also MD), LODR Reg 17 requires at least HALF the Board to be independent, i.e. at least 5 of 9; only 4 are independent
options.B: Yes — independent directors form 4 of 9, which exceeds one-third, the threshold that always applies
options.C: Yes — only two independent directors are required for any listed company
options.D: No — a listed company must have at least 6 independent directors regardless of Board size

questions.explanation: Under LODR Reg 17(1)(b), where the Chairperson is an executive director or a promoter-related person, at least one-half of the Board must comprise independent directors; the one-third test applies only to a company with a non-executive Chairperson. Skyline's Chairperson is also the MD (executive), so it needs ≥1/2 of 9 = at least 5 IDs, but has only 4 — non-compliant. Option B applies the one-third test (the trap for those who miss the executive-chair fact). Option C invents 'two'. Option D invents a flat figure of 6. Determinative facts: executive chairperson + 9-member Board + only 4 IDs.

questions.question: Mr. Sethi was convicted and sentenced to 7 months' imprisonment four months ago. What is the correct position on his disqualification under Sec 164(1)?

options.A: He is not disqualified because the sentence is under one year
options.B: He is disqualified only from Skyline, not from being a director elsewhere
options.C: He is permanently disqualified for life, as any conviction bars directorship forever
options.D: He is disqualified: a sentence of imprisonment of not less than 6 months attracts Sec 164(1)(d), and the disqualification continues for 5 years from expiry of the sentence

questions.explanation: Sec 164(1)(d) disqualifies a person convicted by a court of any offence and sentenced to imprisonment for ≥6 months, with the disqualification running for 5 years from expiry of the sentence. Sethi's 7-month sentence (≥6 months) bites. Option A wrongly treats 'under one year' as safe. Option C confuses this with the proviso that makes disqualification permanent only where the sentence is 7 YEARS or more (a months-vs-years trap). Option B wrongly localises it. Determinative fact: a 7-MONTH sentence, which clears the 6-month line but is far short of the 7-year permanent bar.

questions.question: Because of the three-year non-filing, Skyline's directors are disqualified under Sec 164(2). For a continuing director of Skyline, what is the effect on his office under Sec 167(1)(a)?

options.A: He must immediately vacate office in Skyline itself, but may continue on every other board
options.B: He vacates office in all OTHER companies where he is a director, but (by the proviso to Sec 167(1)(a)) does NOT vacate office in Skyline — the very company whose default caused the Sec 164(2) disqualification
options.C: He vacates office in Skyline and in all other companies simultaneously
options.D: There is no vacation of office; Sec 167 is irrelevant to Sec 164(2) disqualifications

questions.explanation: The proviso to Sec 167(1)(a) (inserted by the 2018 amendment) reverses the intuitive result: where a director is disqualified under Sec 164(2), he vacates office in ALL OTHER companies but continues in the defaulting company itself — so he remains accountable for curing the default. Option A states the exact opposite (the classic trap). Option C ignores the carve-out for the defaulting company. Option D wrongly severs Sec 167 from Sec 164(2). Determinative fact: the disqualification arose from Skyline's own three-year default, so Skyline is the company he does NOT vacate.

questions.question: At the Board meeting to approve the ₹120 crore borrowing, 3 of the 9 directors are interested in that item. What is the minimum number of directors who must be present (and disinterested) to form a valid quorum for that resolution?

options.A: 2 directors, being the statutory floor
options.B: 6 disinterested directors, being two-thirds of the Board
options.C: 5 disinterested directors, i.e. a simple majority of the Board
options.D: 3 disinterested directors — quorum under Sec 174(1) is one-third of total strength (1/3 of 9 = 3) or two, whichever is HIGHER, and interested directors are excluded for that item

questions.explanation: Sec 174(1) fixes quorum at one-third of total strength OR two directors, whichever is HIGHER. One-third of 9 = 3, which exceeds 2, so quorum is 3; and an interested director cannot be counted for the item in which he is interested. Since 6 directors are disinterested, 3 of them present satisfy quorum. Option A applies only the floor of two (ignoring the 'higher' rule). Options C and B invent majority/two-thirds figures. Determinative fact: 9 directors → one-third = 3 (higher than 2).

questions.question: Which statement about Skyline is INCORRECT?

options.A: The 3-day notice for the Board meeting is shorter than the 7 days required by Sec 173(3), and can be validated only if at least one independent director is present
options.B: Capt. Mehra may accept Skyline's directorship, because including Skyline he would hold 10 public-company directorships — exactly at, and not above, the Sec 165 sub-limit of 10
options.C: Because the Chairperson is executive, one-third independent directors suffice for Skyline's Board
options.D: A 7-month sentence attracts disqualification under Sec 164(1)(d)

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option C is false: with an executive chairperson LODR Reg 17 requires at least HALF (not one-third) of the Board to be independent. Option A correctly states the Sec 173(3) shorter-notice rule. Option B is correct — 9 existing public directorships + Skyline = 10, which is exactly at (not above) the Sec 165 public-company sub-limit, and 19 total is within 20. Option D correctly states Sec 164(1)(d). Determinative point: executive-chair triggers the one-half test.

scenarios.scenarioText: Granite Cement Ltd is an unlisted public company with paid-up share capital of ₹40 crore, free reserves of ₹50 crore and a securities premium account of ₹30 crore; it currently has no outstanding borrowings. At a Board meeting the directors propose: (i) to borrow ₹120 crore from a consortium of banks for a new kiln; (ii) to invest ₹95 crore in the equity of an unrelated infrastructure SPV; (iii) to grant a ₹3 crore loan to the spouse of director Mr. Deshmukh; and (iv) to enter a ₹6 crore supply contract with M/s Deshmukh Logistics, a firm in which Mr. Deshmukh is a partner. The company's annual turnover last year was ₹500 crore.

questions.question: Does the proposed ₹120 crore borrowing require shareholder approval under Sec 180(1)(c)?

options.A: No — the borrowing limit is paid-up capital + free reserves + securities premium = ₹120 crore, which the borrowing exactly matches
options.B: Yes — the Sec 180(1)(c) limit is paid-up capital + free reserves = ₹40 cr + ₹50 cr = ₹90 crore (securities premium is EXCLUDED); ₹120 crore exceeds it, so a special resolution is required
options.C: No — a company may always borrow up to three times its net worth without member approval
options.D: Yes — but only an ordinary resolution is needed

questions.explanation: Sec 180(1)(c) requires a special resolution where money to be borrowed (with existing borrowings) exceeds the aggregate of paid-up share capital + free reserves + securities premium... note: the limit for Sec 180 is paid-up capital and free reserves (apart from temporary loans) — securities premium is NOT added for the 180 borrowing ceiling. Limit = ₹40 cr + ₹50 cr = ₹90 crore; ₹120 cr exceeds it → SR needed. Option A wrongly folds in the ₹30 cr securities premium to reach ₹120 cr (the favourite trap — securities premium counts for Sec 186 limits, not the Sec 180 borrowing ceiling). Option C invents a 'three times net worth' rule. Option D wrongly says ordinary resolution. Determinative figures: ₹40 cr + ₹50 cr = ₹90 cr vs ₹120 cr.

questions.question: Does the ₹95 crore investment in the SPV exceed the Sec 186 limit, requiring a special resolution?

options.A: Yes — the Sec 186 ceiling is the HIGHER of 60% of (paid-up + free reserves + securities premium) = ₹72 cr, or 100% of (free reserves + securities premium) = ₹80 cr; the higher is ₹80 crore, and ₹95 crore exceeds it, so a special resolution is required
options.B: No — the limit is 60% of (paid-up + free reserves + securities premium) = ₹72 crore, and ₹95 crore is treated as within board powers
options.C: No — ₹95 crore is below the higher ₹80 crore limit
options.D: Yes — because any investment above ₹50 crore needs a special resolution

questions.explanation: Sec 186(2)/(3): a company may invest/lend up to the HIGHER of (a) 60% of paid-up capital + free reserves + securities premium = 60% × (40+50+30=120) = ₹72 cr, or (b) 100% of free reserves + securities premium = (50+30) = ₹80 cr. The higher is ₹80 cr; ₹95 cr exceeds it → special resolution. Option B takes only the 60% limb (the 'apply-the-lower' trap). Option C miscompares (₹95 cr is ABOVE ₹80 cr). Option D invents a ₹50 cr trigger. Determinative figures: higher of ₹72 cr and ₹80 cr = ₹80 cr vs ₹95 cr.

questions.question: Is the proposed ₹3 crore loan to Mr. Deshmukh's spouse permissible under Sec 185?

options.A: Yes — loans to relatives of directors fall entirely outside Sec 185
options.B: No — Sec 185 bars such loans absolutely, with no exception
options.C: Yes — any loan under ₹5 crore is exempt from Sec 185
options.D: It is prohibited under Sec 185(1) as a loan to a person in whom a director is interested (a spouse is a relative); it can be made only via the Sec 185(2) gateway — prior special resolution plus use by the borrower for its principal business activities

questions.explanation: Sec 185(1) bars a loan to any director or to 'any other person in whom the director is interested', which includes a relative such as a spouse. It is permissible only under Sec 185(2): prior special resolution + the loan being used by the borrower for its principal business activities. Option A wrongly exempts relatives. Option C invents a ₹5 cr threshold. Option B overstates by ignoring the 185(2) exception. Determinative fact: the borrower is a director's spouse.

questions.question: Regarding the ₹6 crore contract with M/s Deshmukh Logistics, which statement is correct under Sec 188?

options.A: Mr. Deshmukh may vote on the Board resolution approving the contract because he is a partner, not a director, of the firm
options.B: It is a related-party transaction; Mr. Deshmukh, being interested, cannot participate in or vote on the Board resolution approving it, and member approval is required if it crosses the prescribed materiality thresholds
options.C: No approval is needed at all because the contract is in the ordinary course of business and at arm's length, which is automatic here
options.D: Only Central Government approval is required for any related-party contract

questions.explanation: A contract with a firm in which a director is a partner is a related-party transaction under Sec 188; the interested director cannot be present/vote on the resolution, and ordinary-resolution (member) approval is needed where prescribed thresholds are crossed. Option A is wrong — interest as a partner still makes him interested. Option C wrongly assumes the ordinary-course/arm's-length exemption without it being established on the facts. Option D imports a CG-approval requirement that the 2015 amendment removed. Determinative fact: Mr. Deshmukh is a partner in the counterparty firm.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a power that Sec 179(3) requires to be exercised only by means of a resolution passed at a Board meeting?

options.A: To borrow monies
options.B: To make loans or give guarantees
options.C: To invest the funds of the company
options.D: To approve the day-to-day purchase of raw materials within delegated authority

questions.explanation: The question seeks the power that is NOT reserved to a Board-meeting resolution. Sec 179(3) reserves, among others, borrowing monies (A), investing the company's funds (C) and making loans/guarantees (B) to resolutions passed at Board meetings (and some may be delegated only to specified committees/officers). Routine day-to-day purchases within delegated authority (D) are ordinary management acts, not Sec 179(3) reserved powers. Determinative point: Sec 179(3) lists borrow/invest/loan as Board-meeting powers; ordinary procurement is not listed.

scenarios.scenarioText: Zephyr Telecom Ltd is a listed company. Orbit Holdings Pvt Ltd currently holds 22% of Zephyr's voting capital. On 5 May 2025 Orbit signs a share-purchase agreement to acquire a further 6%, which would take its holding to 28%. Orbit's nominee on Zephyr's board, Mr. Tandon, is aware of a not-yet-public spectrum-monetisation deal that is likely to move Zephyr's share price sharply. Zephyr's 52-week volume-weighted average price is ₹410, its 26-week VWAP is ₹450, the highest price paid by Orbit in the last 26 weeks is ₹470, and the negotiated SPA price is ₹440. In the following financial year, while holding 30%, Orbit proposes to buy another 4% from the market.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · May 2024] Does Orbit's acquisition taking it from 22% to 28% trigger an open-offer obligation under the SAST Regulations?

options.A: No — an open offer is triggered only on crossing 15% of voting rights, which Orbit crossed long ago
options.B: Yes — acquiring shares/voting rights that, with existing holdings, entitle the acquirer to 25% or more triggers an open offer under Reg 3(1); Orbit crosses 25% (22%→28%)
options.C: No — Orbit is already above 25%, so no fresh trigger arises
options.D: Yes — but only because Orbit is acquiring exactly 6%, the creeping-acquisition cap

questions.explanation: SAST Reg 3(1) triggers an open offer when an acquirer's holding, together with persons acting in concert, reaches 25% or more of voting rights. Orbit moves from 22% (below 25%) to 28% (above 25%), crossing the threshold — open offer triggered. Option A uses the OLD 1997-code trigger of 15% (the amendment trap). Option C is factually wrong — Orbit was at 22%, below 25%. Option D mislabels the move as creeping (creeping applies only when already within the 25%-75% band). Determinative figures: 22% → 28% crosses the 25% line.

questions.question: What is the minimum size of the open offer Orbit must make?

options.A: 20% of the total shares of Zephyr
options.B: 25% of the total shares of Zephyr
options.C: At least 26% of the total shares of Zephyr (the minimum open-offer size under Reg 7)
options.D: Exactly the 6% Orbit is acquiring under the SPA

questions.explanation: Under SAST Reg 7(1) the open offer must be for at least 26% of the total shares of the target. Option A uses 20% (a figure from other contexts, e.g. ICDR MPC lock-in, not the SAST offer size). Option B confuses the offer SIZE with the 25% trigger. Option D wrongly equates offer size with the triggering acquisition. Determinative point: minimum offer size = 26%, distinct from the 25% trigger.

questions.question: Given the prices stated, what is the minimum offer price Orbit must offer in the open offer?

options.A: ₹410, the 52-week VWAP
options.B: ₹470 — the highest of the negotiated price (₹440), the 26-week VWAP (₹450), the 52-week VWAP (₹410) and the highest price paid in the preceding 26 weeks (₹470)
options.C: ₹440, the negotiated SPA price, since that is what Orbit actually agreed to pay
options.D: ₹450, the 26-week VWAP

questions.explanation: SAST Reg 8 fixes the offer price as the HIGHEST of the prescribed parameters — here the negotiated price (₹440), the volume-weighted prices, and the highest price paid by the acquirer in the preceding 26 weeks (₹470). The highest is ₹470. Options A, C and D each pick one lower parameter (the trap of stopping at the negotiated or one VWAP figure). Determinative facts: comparing ₹440, ₹450, ₹410 and ₹470 → ₹470 governs.

questions.question: In the FOLLOWING financial year, while holding 30%, Orbit proposes to acquire a further 4% from the market. Which statement is correct?

options.A: This fresh acquisition again triggers a full open offer, because any further purchase above 25% always does
options.B: It is barred entirely; no acquisition is possible once an acquirer holds 25% or more
options.C: It is permissible under the creeping-acquisition route in Reg 3(2): an acquirer holding between 25% and 75% may acquire up to 5% of voting rights in a financial year without an open offer, and 4% is within that 5% limit
options.D: It is permissible only up to 2% in a financial year

questions.explanation: SAST Reg 3(2) permits an acquirer already holding 25% up to 75% to acquire up to 5% of voting rights in a financial year without triggering an open offer (creeping acquisition). Holding 30%, Orbit's further 4% is within the 5% cap → no open offer. Option A ignores the creeping window. Option B wrongly treats 25% as an absolute ceiling. Option D uses 2% (the continual-disclosure change figure, not the creeping cap). Determinative figures: 30% (within 25-75% band) + 4% ≤ 5% FY cap.

questions.question: Mr. Tandon, possessing the unpublished spectrum-deal information, buys Zephyr shares before it is announced. Which statement is INCORRECT?

options.A: The spectrum-monetisation information is unpublished price-sensitive information (UPSI) under the PIT Regulations
options.B: The maximum monetary penalty for insider trading under Sec 15G of the SEBI Act is capped at ₹1 crore
options.C: Trading while in possession of UPSI is prohibited under PIT Reg 4, regardless of the profit being modest
options.D: Mr. Tandon is an 'insider' because he is a connected person in possession of UPSI

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option B is false: Sec 15G penalises insider trading at the HIGHER of ₹25 crore OR three times the profit made — it is not capped at ₹1 crore (the ₹1 crore cap belongs to Sec 15A/15HB). Options A (UPSI), C (Reg 4 absolute prohibition) and D (connected person in possession = insider) are all correct. Determinative point: 15G = higher of ₹25 cr or 3× profit, not a ₹1 cr cap.

scenarios.scenarioText: Sterling Life Insurance Ltd, an unlisted public company, is making a fresh round of managerial appointments. It proposes to appoint Mr. Khanna, aged 71, as Managing Director for a 5-year term, and Ms. Pillai as a whole-time director. For the year just ended Sterling has inadequate profits (effectively a loss year); its effective capital is ₹60 crore. The Board proposes to pay Mr. Khanna remuneration of ₹96 lakh for the year. Sterling also wishes Mr. Khanna to simultaneously act as Managing Director of two other group companies. A consultant advises the Board that, because it is a loss year, the company may pay 'whatever it likes' since the 11% cap does not operate.

questions.question: Can Mr. Khanna, aged 71, be appointed as Managing Director, and on what condition?

options.A: No — a person above 70 can never be appointed as MD
options.B: Yes — but only with prior Central Government approval
options.C: Yes — a person who has attained 70 years may be appointed MD if a special resolution is passed (with an explanatory statement justifying the appointment); prior Central Government approval is not required for this
options.D: Yes — no special condition applies, since the age limit was abolished

questions.explanation: Sec 196(3)(a) bars appointment/continuation of an MD/WTD/Manager who is below 21 or has attained 70 years, UNLESS a special resolution is passed (the explanatory statement justifying it). Since the 2017 amendment, CG approval is not the route — a special resolution is. Option A is too absolute. Option B uses the pre-2017 CG-approval mechanism (the amendment trap). Option D wrongly says the limit was abolished. Determinative fact: Mr. Khanna is 71 (over 70) → special resolution route.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · May 2023] In this loss/inadequate-profit year, with effective capital of ₹60 crore, can Sterling pay Mr. Khanna ₹96 lakh without a special resolution?

options.A: Yes — for effective capital below ₹100 crore the Schedule V base limit is ₹120 lakh, so ₹96 lakh is comfortably within it
options.B: No — the maximum for this slab is ₹60 lakh and cannot be exceeded even with a special resolution
options.C: Yes — in a loss year there is no monetary ceiling at all on managerial remuneration
options.D: No — for effective capital of ₹5 crore to less than ₹100 crore the Schedule V Part II base yearly limit is ₹84 lakh; ₹96 lakh exceeds it, so it can be paid only by passing a special resolution (which can raise the limit up to double, ₹168 lakh)

questions.explanation: In a loss/inadequate-profit year the Sec 197 percentage limits do not operate; Schedule V Part II governs. For effective capital of ₹5 crore to less than ₹100 crore the base yearly limit is ₹84 lakh, doubled to ₹168 lakh by special resolution. ₹96 lakh exceeds the ₹84 lakh base, so a special resolution is required. Option A uses the ₹120 lakh figure for the NEXT slab (₹100-250 crore) — an adjacent-slab trap. Option C wrongly says no ceiling applies. Option B uses the PRE-amendment ₹60 lakh figure and wrongly treats it as absolute. Determinative figures: ₹60 crore effective capital → ₹84 lakh base; ₹96 lakh > ₹84 lakh.

questions.question: The consultant's advice that 'the 11% cap does not operate, so pay whatever you like' is best described as:

options.A: Correct — Sec 197's overall 11% ceiling simply disappears in a loss year, leaving no limit
options.B: Wholly correct, because Schedule V applies only to listed companies
options.C: Half-right but dangerous: the 11%-of-net-profit ceiling under Sec 197 indeed does not bite in a loss year, but remuneration is then governed and capped by Schedule V Part II, so the company cannot pay 'whatever it likes'
options.D: Wrong — the 11% cap continues to apply even in a loss year

questions.explanation: Sec 197 caps total managerial remuneration at 11% of net profits in a PROFIT year; in a loss/inadequate-profit year that percentage ceiling cannot operate (there is no/low profit), but Schedule V Part II then supplies the applicable monetary limits — so payment is capped, not unlimited. Option A wrongly concludes 'no limit'. Option B falsely restricts Schedule V to listed companies. Option D wrongly says the 11% cap applies in a loss year. Determinative point: loss year → Schedule V caps apply, not 'anything goes'.

questions.question: Can Mr. Khanna simultaneously be the Managing Director of Sterling and of two other group companies?

options.A: A person may be appointed/continue as MD of one company and of one (and only one) other company at the same time — i.e. of at most TWO companies — subject to the conditions in Sec 203(3); MD of three companies is not permitted
options.B: No — a person can be MD of only one company in any circumstance
options.C: Yes — there is no limit on the number of companies in which a person may be MD
options.D: Yes — a person may be MD of up to ten companies, mirroring the directorship sub-limit

questions.explanation: Sec 203(3) permits a whole-time key managerial person to hold office in only one company at a time, with a carve-out allowing an MD/Manager to be the MD/Manager of one other company (so a maximum of two) if specified conditions are met. Being MD of Sterling PLUS two others (three in all) breaches this. Option B is too strict (it ignores the 'one other company' carve-out). Option C wrongly says no limit. Option D imports the Sec 165 directorship sub-limit of 10 (a cross-provision trap). Determinative fact: he wants to be MD of three companies.

questions.question: Which statement is INCORRECT in relation to Sterling's managerial remuneration?

options.A: Sitting fees paid to directors for attending meetings are excluded from the 11% overall managerial-remuneration ceiling
options.B: Where a single managing director is appointed, his remuneration in a profit year cannot exceed 5% of net profits without member approval
options.C: In a loss year a company may exceed the Schedule V limits freely, provided the Board passes a simple Board resolution
options.D: Net profits for Sec 197 are computed in the manner laid down by Sec 198

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option C is false: in a loss year the Schedule V Part II limits apply and can be exceeded only via the prescribed route (special resolution to double the slab limit and satisfaction of conditions) — not by a mere Board resolution. Option A correctly excludes sitting fees from the 11% cap. Option B correctly states the 5% single-MD limit. Option D correctly cites Sec 198 for net-profit computation. Determinative point: Schedule V limits need a special resolution to be exceeded, not a Board resolution.

scenarios.scenarioText: Meridian Ports & Logistics Ltd is suspected of large-scale fund diversion through shell entities. On 10 January 2026 the Central Government assigns the investigation to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) under Sec 212. During the probe the SFIO seeks to question Mr. Iyer, the CFO, and to examine the affairs of Meridian's wholly-owned subsidiary, Coastline Warehousing Ltd, which it believes was used to route funds. Meridian's banker and its external legal adviser are asked to produce documents; both decline citing confidentiality and privilege. The SFIO concludes that an offence under Sec 447 has been committed and wishes to arrest Mr. Iyer. The NCLT later passes an adverse order against Meridian on 1 February 2026; Meridian files its appeal on 20 March 2026.

questions.question: Once the SFIO is investigating an offence under Sec 447, what is the correct position on its power to arrest Mr. Iyer?

options.A: The SFIO has no power of arrest; it must request the local police to arrest
options.B: No arrest is possible because economic offences under the Companies Act are all bailable
options.C: The SFIO can arrest only after obtaining a warrant from a Magistrate
options.D: A designated SFIO officer may arrest a person if he has reason to believe (on the basis of material) that the person is guilty of an offence under Sec 212; the Sec 447 fraud offence is cognizable and bail is subject to the twin conditions in Sec 212(6)

questions.explanation: Sec 212(8) empowers a designated SFIO officer to arrest a person where he has reason to believe (with recorded reasons) the person is guilty; Sec 212(6) makes the Sec 447 offence cognizable and imposes twin conditions for bail (Public Prosecutor's opportunity + the court's satisfaction of innocence and non-repetition). Option A wrongly denies SFIO's arrest power. Option C imports a Magistrate's-warrant requirement that Sec 212(8) does not impose. Option B wrongly characterises the offence as bailable. Determinative fact: an offence under Sec 447 is being investigated by SFIO.

questions.question: Meridian's banker and its external legal adviser both decline to produce documents. Which statement correctly distinguishes their positions?

options.A: A legal adviser cannot be compelled to disclose privileged communications (except the name and address of the client), but a banker is not exempt and can be required to produce documents/information
options.B: Both are fully protected; neither can be compelled to produce anything
options.C: The banker is protected by confidentiality, but the legal adviser must disclose everything including privileged advice
options.D: Both must disclose everything; there is no protection of any kind during an SFIO investigation

questions.explanation: Under the inspection/investigation scheme (Sec 217 read with the privilege protections), a legal adviser retains privilege over professional communications save for the client's name and address, whereas a banker enjoys no such blanket exemption and may be required to produce documents relating to the company. Option B over-protects both. Option C reverses the two positions. Option D wrongly denies all protection. Determinative point: privilege shields the legal adviser's communications, not the banker's records.

questions.question: Can the SFIO extend its investigation to the affairs of the wholly-owned subsidiary, Coastline Warehousing Ltd?

options.A: Yes — the investigation may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, be extended to the affairs of any other body corporate that is or was the company's subsidiary, holding or associate, where relevant to the investigation
options.B: No — each company must be the subject of a separate, independent assignment order
options.C: No — subsidiaries are outside the scope of any SFIO investigation
options.D: Yes — automatically, without any further approval, for any company in the group

questions.explanation: The investigating power extends to related bodies corporate (subsidiary/holding/associate) where relevant, but only with the prior approval of the Central Government (Sec 219). Coastline is a wholly-owned subsidiary suspected of routing funds, so the extension is available with CG approval. Option B wrongly demands a fresh assignment. Option C wrongly excludes subsidiaries. Option D omits the CG-approval condition (the trap of 'automatic' extension). Determinative facts: Coastline is a subsidiary relevant to the fund-routing.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · Nov 2022] The NCLT order is dated 1 February 2026 and Meridian files its appeal to the NCLAT on 20 March 2026. Is the appeal maintainable on limitation?

options.A: Yes — the appeal lies within 45 days; though filed on day 47 (just beyond 45 days), the NCLAT may condone a further delay of up to 45 days on sufficient cause, so it is within the maximum 90-day outer limit
options.B: No — the 30-day appeal period expired, and there is no power to condone
options.C: No — the appeal had to be filed within 60 days and is time-barred
options.D: Yes — there is no limitation period for appeals to the NCLAT

questions.explanation: Sec 421(3) gives 45 days to appeal to the NCLAT; the proviso allows condonation of a further period not exceeding 45 days on sufficient cause (maximum 90 days). From 1 Feb to 20 Mar is 47 days — beyond 45 but within the condonable 90-day outer limit, so it is maintainable if sufficient cause is shown. Option B uses a wrong 30-day period and denies condonation. Option C uses 60 days. Option D wrongly says no limitation. Determinative facts: 1 Feb → 20 Mar = 47 days, within 45 + 45 = 90.

questions.question: If Meridian loses before the NCLAT and wishes to approach the Supreme Court, which statement is INCORRECT?

options.A: A pure question of fact decided by the NCLAT can be re-agitated before the Supreme Court under Sec 423
options.B: An appeal to the Supreme Court under Sec 423 lies only on a question of law arising out of the NCLAT order
options.C: The appeal to the Supreme Court must ordinarily be filed within 60 days of the NCLAT order
options.D: No civil court has jurisdiction over matters the NCLT/NCLAT is empowered to determine

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option A is false: Sec 423 confines the Supreme Court appeal to a QUESTION OF LAW; pure questions of fact cannot be re-agitated. Option B correctly states the question-of-law limit. Option C correctly states the 60-day period. Option D correctly states the civil-court bar (Sec 430). Determinative point: Sec 423 = question of law only.

scenarios.scenarioText: Helios Solar Energy Ltd defaults on its obligations. GreenVolt Components Ltd, an operational creditor, is owed ₹1.2 crore for supplied inverters and has received no payment. A consortium bank, which is a financial creditor, is owed ₹40 crore. GreenVolt serves a demand notice; Helios neither pays nor raises a pre-existing dispute. CIRP is admitted, a moratorium is declared and a resolution professional takes charge. The Committee of Creditors considers a resolution plan that secures 64% of the voting share. Separately, Mr. Helios, the promoter who had given a personal guarantee for the consortium loan (now invoked), wishes to submit his own resolution plan. On liquidation, the company has workmen's dues, employees' dues and secured-creditor claims to rank.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · May 2023] Is GreenVolt's claim of ₹1.2 crore sufficient to maintain an application to initiate CIRP against Helios?

options.A: No — the minimum default threshold is ₹1 lakh, which is met, but operational creditors cannot apply at all
options.B: Yes — the minimum default threshold under Sec 4 is ₹1 crore (raised in 2020 from ₹1 lakh), and GreenVolt's ₹1.2 crore default exceeds it
options.C: No — the threshold is ₹1 crore but the default of ₹1.2 crore is disputed by operation of law
options.D: Yes — because any default above ₹1 lakh, the original threshold, is enough

questions.explanation: Sec 4 sets the minimum default at ₹1 crore (raised from ₹1 lakh by the March 2020 notification). GreenVolt's ₹1.2 crore default exceeds ₹1 crore, so the application is maintainable; operational creditors can apply under Sec 9 after the demand-notice procedure. Option A wrongly uses ₹1 lakh and wrongly bars operational creditors. Option C invents a dispute (the facts say no pre-existing dispute). Option D uses the pre-2020 ₹1 lakh figure (the amendment trap, which also collides with the Companies Act Sec 271(a) ₹1 lakh). Determinative figure: ₹1.2 crore vs the ₹1 crore threshold.

questions.question: What procedural step distinguishes GreenVolt's route (as an operational creditor) from the consortium bank's route (as a financial creditor) to initiate CIRP?

options.A: Both must serve a 21-day demand notice before filing
options.B: GreenVolt (operational creditor) must first serve a demand notice giving Helios 10 days to pay or dispute; the financial creditor need not serve any demand notice and may apply directly under Sec 7
options.C: Only the financial creditor must serve a demand notice; the operational creditor applies directly
options.D: Neither needs to give any notice; both apply directly to the NCLT

questions.explanation: An operational creditor must serve a demand notice under Sec 8 and wait the prescribed period (10 days) for payment or notice of a pre-existing dispute before filing under Sec 9; a financial creditor files directly under Sec 7 without any demand notice. Option A wrongly applies a notice to both. Option C reverses the rule. Option D wrongly says neither needs notice. Determinative point: demand notice is an operational-creditor requirement, not a financial-creditor one.

questions.question: The resolution plan secures 64% of the CoC's voting share. Can the NCLT sanction it?

options.A: Yes — a plan approved by more than 50% of the voting share is valid
options.B: No — a resolution plan must be approved by at least 66% of the voting share of the Committee of Creditors; 64% falls short, so it cannot be put forward for NCLT approval
options.C: Yes — 64% exceeds the required 51% threshold
options.D: No — the plan needs 75% of the voting share, the figure that has always applied

questions.explanation: Under Sec 30(4)/Sec 31, a resolution plan requires approval by at least 66% of the CoC voting share before it can be submitted to the NCLT. 64% is below 66%, so the plan fails. Option A and C use 50%/51% (ordinary-resolution-style thresholds that do not apply). Option D uses the pre-2019 figure of 75% (the amendment trap). Determinative figure: 64% < 66%.

questions.question: Mr. Helios, the promoter who personally guaranteed the consortium loan that has been invoked, wishes to submit a resolution plan. Is he eligible under Sec 29A?

options.A: Yes — promoters are always free to submit resolution plans for their own companies
options.B: Yes — personal guarantors are expressly carved out of Sec 29A
options.C: No — Sec 29A renders a person ineligible if he has executed a guarantee in favour of a creditor in respect of the corporate debtor and that guarantee has been invoked and remains unpaid; Mr. Helios falls within this disqualification
options.D: No — but only because he is a promoter, irrespective of the guarantee

questions.explanation: Sec 29A(h) disqualifies a person who has executed a guarantee in favour of a creditor in respect of a corporate debtor under CIRP, where that guarantee has been invoked and remains unpaid. Mr. Helios's personal guarantee for the consortium loan has been invoked, so he is ineligible. Option A wrongly says promoters are always free. Option B wrongly claims a carve-out for guarantors. Option D gives the wrong reason (promoter status per se is not the bar; the invoked, unpaid guarantee is). Determinative fact: his guarantee was invoked and is unpaid.

questions.question: On liquidation, which statement about the Sec 53 waterfall is INCORRECT?

options.A: Unpaid dues owed to workmen rank for the 12 months preceding liquidation, while other employees' dues are taken for 24 months
options.B: Wages and unpaid dues of employees (other than workmen) are taken for the period of 12 months preceding liquidation
options.C: Workmen's dues for the period of 24 months preceding liquidation rank equally (pari passu) with secured creditors who have relinquished their security
options.D: Insolvency resolution process costs and liquidation costs are paid in full ahead of all other claims

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option A reverses the periods: under Sec 53, WORKMEN's dues are reckoned for 24 months (and rank with secured creditors), while OTHER EMPLOYEES' dues are reckoned for 12 months. Option C correctly states the 24-month workmen/secured pari passu rank. Option B correctly states the 12-month employee period. Option D correctly puts CIRP/liquidation costs first. Determinative point: workmen = 24 months, employees = 12 months (not reversed).

scenarios.scenarioText: Anandam Sugars Ltd is in financial distress. A trade creditor, Mr. Pawar, served a statutory demand for ₹90,000 which has remained unpaid for 25 days. Separately, the members of Anandam pass a special resolution that the company be wound up by the Tribunal. The directors are considering a members' voluntary winding up and have prepared a declaration of solvency stating that the company will be able to pay its debts in full within 3.5 years. The Registrar of Companies, suspecting that Anandam's affairs were conducted fraudulently, wishes to petition the Tribunal for winding up on that ground. A rival argues that the company should instead be wound up on just-and-equitable grounds.

questions.question: Does Mr. Pawar's unpaid demand of ₹90,000 (unpaid for 25 days) establish that Anandam is 'unable to pay its debts' for a Tribunal winding-up petition under Sec 271(a)/Sec 271?

options.A: No — the statutory demand must be for a sum exceeding ₹1 lakh; ₹90,000 falls below the threshold, so it does not by itself establish inability to pay
options.B: Yes — any unpaid demand outstanding for more than 21 days proves inability to pay
options.C: Yes — the threshold is ₹1 crore and ₹90,000, being a clear default, suffices
options.D: No — because the threshold is ₹1 crore and ₹90,000 is below it

questions.explanation: Under the Companies Act, the demand-based 'inability to pay debts' route requires a debt exceeding ₹1 lakh remaining unpaid for 21 days after demand. Mr. Pawar's ₹90,000 is below ₹1 lakh, so it does not establish inability to pay — regardless of the 25-day delay. Option B ignores the monetary floor. Option C uses ₹1 crore (the IBC threshold — a deliberate cross-law trap) and wrongly concludes it suffices. Option D cites the IBC ₹1 crore figure rather than the Companies Act ₹1 lakh; though its conclusion (insufficient) is right, the reasoning is wrong, making A the correct statement. Determinative figures: ₹90,000 < ₹1 lakh (Companies Act), not the ₹1 crore IBC figure.

questions.question: The members have passed a special resolution that Anandam be wound up by the Tribunal. Is that a valid independent ground for a Tribunal winding-up petition?

options.A: Yes — Sec 271(b) makes it a ground that the company has, by special resolution, resolved that it be wound up by the Tribunal
options.B: No — members cannot ever ask the Tribunal to wind up their own company
options.C: No — a special resolution can only lead to a voluntary winding up, never a Tribunal winding up
options.D: Yes — but only an ordinary resolution is required for this ground

questions.explanation: Sec 271(b) expressly lists, as a ground for compulsory (Tribunal) winding up, that the company has by SPECIAL RESOLUTION resolved to be wound up by the Tribunal. Option B wrongly denies the ground. Option C wrongly confines special resolutions to voluntary winding up. Option D wrongly downgrades the requirement to an ordinary resolution. Determinative fact: a special resolution for Tribunal winding up was passed.

questions.question: The declaration of solvency states that Anandam will pay its debts in full within 3.5 years. Is this declaration valid for a members' voluntary winding up?

options.A: Yes — there is no time limit on the period stated in a declaration of solvency
options.B: No — the declaration must state that the company will be able to pay its debts in full within a period not exceeding 3 years from commencement of the winding up; a 3.5-year period is impermissible
options.C: Yes — the permissible period is 5 years and 3.5 years is well within it
options.D: No — the permissible period is only 1 year

questions.explanation: A declaration of solvency must state that the company will be able to pay its debts in full within a period not exceeding 3 years from the commencement of winding up. A stated period of 3.5 years exceeds the 3-year ceiling and is invalid. Option A wrongly says no limit. Option C uses 5 years. Option D uses 1 year. Determinative figure: 3.5 years > the 3-year statutory ceiling.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · Nov 2023] Can the Registrar of Companies present a winding-up petition on the ground that Anandam's affairs were conducted fraudulently?

options.A: No — although the Registrar is a competent petitioner generally, he is barred from petitioning on the 'fraudulent/unlawful conduct' ground (and on the special-resolution ground); a fraud-based petition cannot be presented by the Registrar
options.B: Yes — the Registrar may petition on any of the grounds available under Sec 271
options.C: Yes — the Registrar is in fact the only authority that can petition on the fraud ground
options.D: No — the Registrar can never present a winding-up petition on any ground

questions.explanation: Sec 272 lists the Registrar among competent petitioners but expressly bars him from petitioning on the grounds in Sec 271 clause (b) (special resolution) and clause (d) (affairs conducted in a fraudulent/unlawful manner). A fraud-based petition is therefore not open to the Registrar. Option B ignores the carve-out. Option C wrongly makes the Registrar the exclusive fraud-petitioner. Option D wrongly bars the Registrar entirely. Determinative point: Registrar cannot petition on the fraud ground (clause (d)).

questions.question: Which statement regarding Anandam's winding up is INCORRECT?

options.A: Where a declaration of solvency is duly made and delivered, the winding up proceeds as a members' voluntary winding up
options.B: An unpaid statutory demand of ₹90,000 satisfies the monetary threshold for the 'inability to pay debts' ground
options.C: 'Just and equitable' is a recognised ground on which the Tribunal may order winding up
options.D: A special resolution to be wound up by the Tribunal is itself a ground under Sec 271

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option B is false: ₹90,000 is below the ₹1 lakh demand threshold, so it does not satisfy the inability-to-pay ground. Option A correctly states the effect of a valid declaration of solvency. Option C correctly lists 'just and equitable' (Sec 271(e)/(f)). Option D correctly states the special-resolution ground (Sec 271(b)). Determinative point: ₹90,000 is below ₹1 lakh.

scenarios.scenarioText: Beacon Media & Broadcasting Ltd is a listed company. Its trading window for the quarter is closed from quarter-end until the financial results are declared. Ms. Rao, the CFO, is aware of an unpublished, advanced merger negotiation that will materially affect Beacon's share price. The results for the quarter are declared on 12 May 2026 at 4:00 pm. Ms. Rao trades in Beacon shares on 13 May 2026 at 10:00 am and again separately under a 'trading plan' she had formulated. From her dealings she makes a profit of ₹9 crore. SEBI initiates proceedings; it also considers a separate disgorgement direction and the possibility of criminal prosecution.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · May 2024] The results are declared on 12 May at 4:00 pm and Ms. Rao trades on 13 May at 10:00 am. Is her trade within the permitted (re-opened) trading window?

options.A: Yes — the window reopens immediately upon declaration of results, so trading the next morning is fine
options.B: Yes — the window reopens 24 hours after the board meeting approving the results
options.C: No — the trading window reopens only 48 hours after the results are declared; trading at 10:00 am on 13 May (about 18 hours later) is still within the closure period and is prohibited
options.D: No — the window reopens 72 hours after declaration, so the trade is premature

questions.explanation: Under the PIT trading-window norms, the window closed at quarter-end reopens only 48 hours AFTER the unpublished price-sensitive information (here the financial results) becomes generally available. Results were declared at 4:00 pm on 12 May; 48 hours later is 4:00 pm on 14 May. A trade at 10:00 am on 13 May (≈18 hours later) is within the closure and prohibited. Option A wrongly says 'immediately'. Option B uses 24 hours and refers to the board meeting rather than declaration. Option D uses 72 hours. Determinative facts: declaration 12 May 4 pm; trade 13 May 10 am, well within 48 hours.

questions.question: For the trades under her formulated 'trading plan', what cooling-off period must have elapsed before implementation can commence?

options.A: The trading plan can be implemented immediately on approval, with no cooling-off
options.B: Trading under the plan may commence after a cooling-off of 6 months from approval
options.C: Trading under the plan may commence after 120 TRADING days from approval
options.D: Trading under the plan may commence only after 120 CALENDAR days from the public disclosure of the plan

questions.explanation: PIT Reg 5 requires that a trading plan be publicly disclosed and that trading under it commence only after a cooling-off period of 120 CALENDAR days from the public disclosure. Option A wrongly removes the cooling-off. Option C swaps 'calendar' for 'trading' days (a common trap, colliding with the SAST/board-meeting day-counting conventions). Option B uses 6 months. Determinative point: 120 calendar days from public disclosure.

questions.question: From her insider dealing Ms. Rao makes a profit of ₹9 crore. What is the maximum monetary penalty SEBI can levy under Sec 15G for insider trading?

options.A: ₹25 crore, being the fixed statutory ceiling
options.B: ₹1 crore, the general penalty cap
options.C: ₹9 crore, being the amount of profit she made
options.D: ₹27 crore — the penalty is the HIGHER of ₹25 crore or three times the profit made (3 × ₹9 crore = ₹27 crore), so ₹27 crore applies

questions.explanation: Sec 15G fixes the insider-trading penalty at the HIGHER of ₹25 crore OR three times the amount of profit made. Three times ₹9 crore = ₹27 crore, which exceeds ₹25 crore, so the penalty can be ₹27 crore. Option A wrongly treats ₹25 crore as a fixed ceiling rather than a floor. Option C uses the bare profit. Option B uses the ₹1 crore cap from Sec 15A/15HB (a cross-provision trap). Determinative figure: 3 × ₹9 crore = ₹27 crore > ₹25 crore.

questions.question: Beacon's counsel argues that because SEBI is levying a Sec 15G penalty, it cannot also seek disgorgement or pursue criminal prosecution. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Correct — a Sec 15G penalty is the sole remedy and excludes all others
options.B: Incorrect — SEBI's power to direct disgorgement of unlawful gains (under Sec 11B) and the possibility of criminal prosecution under Sec 24 are independent of, and can run alongside, an adjudication penalty under Sec 15G
options.C: Correct — disgorgement is merely another name for the Sec 15G penalty
options.D: Incorrect — but only criminal prosecution is barred; disgorgement is excluded

questions.explanation: Disgorgement under Sec 11B (recovering unlawful gains) and criminal prosecution under Sec 24 are distinct from an adjudicating officer's monetary penalty under Sec 15G; they can co-exist. Option A wrongly treats the penalty as exclusive. Option C wrongly equates disgorgement with the penalty (disgorgement strips the wrongful gain; it is not a penalty). Option D wrongly bars one of the two. Determinative point: Sec 15G penalty, Sec 11B disgorgement and Sec 24 prosecution are independent remedies.

questions.question: Which statement about Ms. Rao's position under the PIT Regulations is INCORRECT?

options.A: As CFO aware of the merger negotiation, she is an 'insider' both as a connected person and as a person in possession of UPSI
options.B: The advanced, unpublished merger negotiation qualifies as unpublished price-sensitive information
options.C: Because she is a connected person, she may trade during the closed window provided she later discloses the trade
options.D: Trading while in possession of UPSI is prohibited under PIT Reg 4 irrespective of motive

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option C is false: subsequent disclosure does not cure trading during a closed window or while in possession of UPSI — the prohibition is absolute. Option A correctly identifies her as an insider on both limbs. Option B correctly treats the merger negotiation as UPSI. Option D correctly states the Reg 4 absolute prohibition. Determinative point: post-trade disclosure does not legitimise prohibited insider trading.

scenarios.scenarioText: Lustre Gems & Jewellery Ltd, based in Surat, exports polished diamonds. Mr. Verma, its export head, was physically present in India for only 150 days during the preceding financial year (April–March), having spent the rest of the year managing buyers in Antwerp; the year before that he was in India for 320 days. Lustre exports a consignment worth USD 4 million and is deciding when its proceeds must be brought back. Separately, Mr. Verma wishes to remit USD 3,00,000 in the financial year for his daughter's overseas education, and Lustre is considering acquiring a showroom property in Dubai. A contravention of FEMA involving a clearly quantifiable sum of ₹10 crore is also under examination.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · Nov 2022] For the preceding financial year, what is Mr. Verma's residential status under FEMA, given 150 days' presence in India that year?

options.A: Resident — he was present for more than 182 days in India in the relevant period
options.B: Resident — because he is an Indian citizen, citizenship determines FEMA residence
options.C: Resident — because residential status under FEMA is determined on the calendar-year basis and he was here 320 days the year before
options.D: Person resident OUTSIDE India for that year — FEMA's test counts presence in the PRECEDING FINANCIAL YEAR (April–March), and 150 days does not exceed 182 days, so he is not a person resident in India

questions.explanation: Sec 2(v) defines a person resident in India primarily as one residing in India for MORE than 182 days during the PRECEDING FINANCIAL YEAR (April–March). Mr. Verma's 150 days does not exceed 182, so for that year he is a person resident outside India. Option A misstates 150 as exceeding 182. Option C wrongly uses the calendar-year basis (the Companies Act resident-director test uses the calendar year — a deliberate cross-law trap) and irrelevantly relies on the prior year. Option B wrongly equates citizenship with FEMA residence. Determinative facts: 150 days (≤182) in the preceding FINANCIAL year.

questions.question: Lustre exports diamonds worth USD 4 million. What is the correct position on realisation and repatriation of the export proceeds?

options.A: There is no obligation to bring back export proceeds once goods leave India
options.B: Export proceeds must be repatriated within 30 days of shipment, failing which the export is void
options.C: Export proceeds may be retained abroad indefinitely so long as they are eventually declared
options.D: Under Sec 7, the exporter must furnish prescribed particulars and realise and repatriate the export value to India within the period prescribed by RBI (generally nine months from export)

questions.explanation: Sec 7 obliges an exporter to declare the full export value and to realise and repatriate the proceeds to India within the period and manner prescribed by the RBI (the general timeline being nine months). Option A wrongly denies any obligation. Option C wrongly permits indefinite retention. Option B invents a 30-day period and a 'void export' consequence. Determinative point: realisation/repatriation within the RBI-prescribed period, not 'never' or '30 days'.

questions.question: Regarding Mr. Verma's proposed remittance of USD 3,00,000 for his daughter's education, and Lustre's proposed Dubai showroom, which statement is correct?

options.A: Both are current account transactions and are freely permitted without limit
options.B: Both are capital account transactions, freely permitted
options.C: The education remittance is a current account transaction (generally permitted), but it exceeds the Liberalised Remittance Scheme limit of USD 2,50,000 per financial year, so the excess needs RBI approval; acquiring overseas immovable property is a capital account transaction and is permitted only as allowed by RBI
options.D: The education remittance is a capital account transaction, and the Dubai property is a current account transaction

questions.explanation: Current account transactions (e.g. education remittances) are generally permitted but the LRS caps remittances by a resident individual at USD 2,50,000 per financial year; USD 3,00,000 exceeds it, so the excess needs RBI approval. Acquiring immovable property outside India alters assets outside India and is a capital account transaction (Sec 6) permitted only to the extent allowed by RBI. Option A ignores the LRS cap. Option B mislabels both as capital. Option D reverses the two classifications. Determinative figures: USD 3,00,000 > USD 2,50,000 LRS limit; overseas property = capital account.

questions.question: For the FEMA contravention involving a quantifiable amount of ₹10 crore, what is the maximum monetary penalty under Sec 13?

options.A: A flat ₹2 lakh, since that is the standard FEMA penalty
options.B: Up to ₹10 crore only, the exact sum involved
options.C: Up to three times the sum involved where the amount is quantifiable — i.e. up to ₹30 crore (3 × ₹10 crore)
options.D: Up to ₹5,000 per day, with no other ceiling

questions.explanation: Sec 13(1) provides that where the contravention involves a quantifiable amount, the penalty may extend to up to three times that sum; for ₹10 crore that is up to ₹30 crore. Option A uses the ₹2 lakh figure that applies only where the amount is NOT quantifiable. Option B caps it at the bare sum. Option D uses the ₹5,000-per-day continuing-contravention add-on as if it were the only penalty. Determinative figure: quantifiable ₹10 crore → up to 3× = ₹30 crore.

questions.question: Which statement under FEMA is INCORRECT?

options.A: A current account transaction is generally permitted unless the Central Government restricts it in public interest
options.B: A capital account transaction is generally prohibited unless permitted by the RBI
options.C: Where the amount of a contravention is not quantifiable, the penalty may extend to ₹2 lakh
options.D: FEMA's 182-day residence test is computed on a calendar-year (January–December) basis

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option D is false: FEMA's 182-day test uses the PRECEDING FINANCIAL YEAR (April–March), not the calendar year (the calendar-year basis belongs to the Companies Act resident-director test). Option A correctly states the current-account rule (Sec 5). Option B correctly states the capital-account rule (Sec 6). Option C correctly states the ₹2 lakh non-quantifiable penalty (Sec 13). Determinative point: FEMA = financial year, not calendar year.

scenarios.scenarioText: Crescent Petrochemicals Ltd proposes a scheme of arrangement with its creditors and members. At the court-convened meeting of equity shareholders, the scheme is approved by shareholders representing the requisite value present and voting. A dissenting group of shareholders holding 8% of the company's shareholding, and a group of creditors holding 4% of the total outstanding debt, wish to object to the scheme. Crescent separately seeks to dispense with a creditors' meeting on the strength of affidavits from creditors representing 88% in value of the company's debt. Crescent also proposes a cross-border merger in which it will merge into Pacifica Chemicals Pte Ltd, a company incorporated in Singapore (a notified jurisdiction). The last financial year of Crescent ended 8 months before the first scheme meeting.

questions.question: What is the approval threshold for the scheme at each class meeting under Sec 230?

options.A: A simple majority in number of those present and voting
options.B: Ninety per cent in value of those present and voting
options.C: Three-fourths in number of the total members of the company
options.D: A majority in number representing three-fourths (75%) in VALUE of the creditors or members (or class) present and voting

questions.explanation: Sec 230(6) requires approval by a majority of persons representing three-fourths in VALUE of the creditors/members (or class) present and voting, in person or by proxy. Option A drops the 75%-value requirement. Option C wrongly applies '3/4 in number of total members'. Option B uses 90% (the figure for the meeting-dispensation affidavit route under Sec 230(9), not the approval threshold). Determinative point: 3/4 in value of those present and voting.

questions.question: Can the dissenting 8% shareholders and the 4% creditors maintain objections to the scheme under Sec 230(4)?

options.A: Yes — any single shareholder or creditor may object to a scheme
options.B: No — an objection can be made only by persons holding at least 10% of the shareholding (shareholders) or at least 5% of the total outstanding debt (creditors); 8% shareholding and 4% of debt both fall below these thresholds
options.C: Yes — because together they exceed 10% of the combined capital and debt
options.D: No — the thresholds are 5% for shareholders and 10% for creditors, and they fail those

questions.explanation: Sec 230(4) permits objections only by persons holding not less than 10% of the shareholding (members) or not less than 5% of the total outstanding debt (creditors). The dissenters hold 8% shareholding (<10%) and 4% of debt (<5%), so neither group can object. Option A ignores the thresholds. Option C wrongly aggregates two different classes. Option D reverses the two percentages (5% for shareholders / 10% for creditors). Determinative figures: 8% < 10% (members) and 4% < 5% (creditors).

questions.question: Can Crescent dispense with the creditors' meeting on the strength of affidavits from creditors representing 88% in value of its debt?

options.A: No — a meeting of creditors may be dispensed with only where creditors representing at least 90% in value agree by way of affidavit; 88% falls short of the 90% requirement
options.B: Yes — affidavits from a majority in value (over 75%) are sufficient to dispense with the meeting
options.C: Yes — 88% exceeds the two-thirds threshold required for dispensation
options.D: No — dispensation requires unanimous (100%) creditor affidavits

questions.explanation: Sec 230(9) allows the Tribunal to dispense with a meeting of creditors where creditors having at least 90% value agree and confirm by affidavit. 88% is below 90%, so the meeting cannot be dispensed with. Option B uses 75%. Option C uses two-thirds. Option D overstates it as 100%. Determinative figure: 88% < 90%.

questions.question: For Crescent's merger into the Singapore company Pacifica Chemicals Pte Ltd, which statement is correct under Sec 234?

options.A: Only NCLT approval is needed; cross-border mergers are treated identically to domestic mergers
options.B: A cross-border merger requires the prior approval of the RBI in addition to NCLT sanction, and is permitted only with companies in jurisdictions notified by the Central Government — and Singapore is a notified jurisdiction
options.C: Only RBI approval is needed; the NCLT has no role in a cross-border merger
options.D: Cross-border mergers with any foreign company are freely permitted without RBI or NCLT involvement

questions.explanation: Sec 234 read with the rules permits cross-border mergers only with companies in jurisdictions notified by the Central Government and requires prior RBI approval in addition to NCLT sanction. Singapore is a notified jurisdiction, so the merger can proceed with RBI approval + NCLT sanction. Option A omits the RBI approval/notified-jurisdiction conditions. Option C wrongly removes the NCLT. Option D wrongly says no approvals at all. Determinative facts: cross-border (Singapore, notified) → RBI + NCLT.

questions.question: Crescent's last financial year ended 8 months before the first scheme meeting. Which statement is INCORRECT?

options.A: Because the last accounts are more than 6 months old, Crescent must annex supplementary (interim) accounts for the merger meeting
options.B: A certified copy of the Tribunal's order sanctioning the scheme must be filed with the Registrar within 30 days
options.C: The transferee company cannot, as a result of the scheme, hold its own shares; any such shares of the transferor must be cancelled
options.D: Since the accounts are only 8 months old, no supplementary accounts are required as the limit is 12 months

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option D is false: where the last annual accounts ended MORE THAN 6 MONTHS before the first meeting, supplementary/interim accounts must be annexed — the limit is 6 months, not 12. Option A correctly applies the 6-month rule (8 months > 6 → supplementary accounts needed). Option B correctly states the 30-day RoC filing. Option C correctly states the no-treasury-shares rule on merger. Determinative figure: 8 months > the 6-month threshold.

scenarios.scenarioText: Nirvana Healthcare Hospitals Ltd is a company having a share capital, with a total of 800 members. A faction of 75 members, together holding 8% of the issued share capital, alleges that the controlling group is running the company's affairs in a manner oppressive to the minority and prejudicial to the company. They wish to apply to the Tribunal under Sec 241. Among the impugned acts, the controlling group had the Tribunal-appointed earlier terminate the 5-year service agreement of an ousted director, Dr. Sen, who now claims ₹2 crore compensation from the company. The faction also wants to bring a class action against the company's statutory auditor for certifying manipulated accounts. An adverse Tribunal order is later passed and the losing side considers an appeal.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · May 2023] Do the 75 members holding 8% meet the eligibility threshold to apply under Sec 241/244 without a waiver?

options.A: Yes — 75 members is sufficient because only 50 members are needed
options.B: No — they need at least one-fifth of the members, which they do not have
options.C: Yes — 8% of the issued capital is sufficient because the requirement is only 5%
options.D: No — for a company with share capital, the applicants must be at least 100 members OR members holding at least one-tenth (10%) of the issued capital, whichever is LESS; here 75 members (<100) and 8% (<10%) meet neither limb

questions.explanation: Sec 244(1)(a) requires, for a company with share capital, applicants numbering at least 100 members OR holding at least 1/10th (10%) of the issued capital, whichever is LESS. The faction is 75 members (below 100) and holds 8% (below 10%) — failing both limbs. Option A invents a 50-member rule. Option C uses 5% (the Sec 245 class-action third alternative, not Sec 244). Option B uses the 1/5 figure that applies to companies WITHOUT share capital. Determinative figures: 75 < 100 and 8% < 10%.

questions.question: Given they fall short of the Sec 244 threshold, is there any route by which the 75 members can still maintain the oppression petition?

options.A: No — the eligibility threshold is absolute and can never be relaxed
options.B: Yes — but only the Central Government, not the Tribunal, can grant such a waiver
options.C: Yes — the Tribunal has a discretionary power to WAIVE the Sec 244 eligibility requirements on an application, permitting the members to proceed
options.D: No — they must instead approach the High Court directly

questions.explanation: The proviso to Sec 244(1) empowers the TRIBUNAL to waive the numerical/shareholding requirements on an application, allowing otherwise-ineligible members to apply. Option A wrongly treats the threshold as absolute (it is waivable, unlike the Sec 245 class-action thresholds). Option B wrongly assigns the waiver to the Central Government. Option D wrongly routes them to the High Court. Determinative point: Sec 244 thresholds are Tribunal-waivable.

questions.question: Dr. Sen, whose 5-year service agreement was terminated pursuant to a Tribunal order, claims ₹2 crore compensation from Nirvana. Is the claim sustainable?

options.A: Yes — wrongful termination always entitles a director to compensation for the unexpired term
options.B: No — but he may instead claim the compensation from the individual directors personally
options.C: Yes — he is entitled to ₹2 crore being the salary for the unexpired portion of the 5-year term
options.D: No — where the Tribunal's order terminates or modifies an agreement, Sec 243 bars the affected managerial person from claiming compensation or damages for loss of office from the company

questions.explanation: Sec 243(1)(b)/(2) provides that where an agreement is terminated or set aside under a Tribunal order in oppression/mismanagement proceedings, no managing/whole-time director or manager so removed is entitled to claim damages or compensation for loss of office against the company. Dr. Sen's ₹2 crore claim therefore fails. Options A and C wrongly assume an entitlement for the unexpired term. Option B wrongly redirects the claim to directors personally. Determinative fact: the agreement was terminated under a Tribunal order.

questions.question: Regarding the proposed class action against Nirvana's statutory auditor, which statement is correct under Sec 245?

options.A: A class action can be brought only against the company and its directors, never against the auditor
options.B: A class action lies only before the High Court, not the Tribunal
options.C: A class action against the auditor is permissible, but the Tribunal may waive its eligibility thresholds just as under Sec 244
options.D: A class action may be brought against the company's auditor (including the audit firm) for an improper or misleading statement or fraudulent/unlawful conduct, and the Sec 245 thresholds — unlike Sec 244 — cannot be waived by the Tribunal

questions.explanation: Sec 245 expressly permits a class action against the company's auditor/audit firm (and experts/advisers) for misleading statements or fraudulent/unlawful conduct, and — unlike Sec 244 — the Sec 245 eligibility thresholds are NOT waivable. Option A wrongly excludes the auditor. Option C wrongly imports the Sec 244 waiver into Sec 245. Option B wrongly assigns it to the High Court (it lies before the Tribunal). Determinative point: auditor is a proper respondent; no waiver under Sec 245.

questions.question: Which statement about the Tribunal's powers and the appeal is INCORRECT?

options.A: In oppression/mismanagement proceedings the Tribunal may, as a remedy, order the winding up of the company
options.B: An appeal against the Tribunal's final order lies to the NCLAT
options.C: Because winding up is involved, an aggrieved party must appeal directly to the High Court rather than the NCLAT
options.D: The Tribunal may regulate the conduct of the company's affairs and may order purchase of the minority's shares

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option C is false: appeals from NCLT orders lie to the NCLAT (Sec 421), not to the High Court, even where winding up is ordered as a remedy. Option A correctly states that Sec 242 permits winding up as a remedy. Option B correctly states the NCLAT appeal route. Option D correctly lists Tribunal powers under Sec 242. Determinative point: appeal lies to NCLAT, not High Court.

scenarios.scenarioText: QuickBasket Marketplace Ltd is a listed e-commerce company. Its Board has 8 directors, and its Chairperson is an executive director. The Board currently has 3 independent directors. Its Audit Committee comprises 3 members, of whom only 1 is an independent director, and is chaired by a non-independent director. For the year, QuickBasket's consolidated turnover is ₹9,000 crore. It proposes a related-party transaction with its promoter group worth ₹950 crore. Its quarterly (standalone and consolidated) financial results for the quarter ended 30 June were submitted to the stock exchanges on the 50th day after quarter-end. The company is among the top 1,500 listed entities by market capitalisation.

questions.question: Is QuickBasket's Board composition (8 directors, executive Chairperson, 3 independent directors) compliant with LODR Reg 17?

options.A: Yes — three independent directors is always sufficient for any listed company
options.B: No — with an executive Chairperson, at least half the Board must be independent, i.e. at least 4 of 8; only 3 are independent
options.C: Yes — only one-third of the Board (about 3) need be independent here
options.D: No — a listed company must have at least 5 independent directors irrespective of Board size

questions.explanation: LODR Reg 17(1)(b): where the Chairperson is an executive director, at least one-half of the Board must comprise independent directors. Half of 8 = 4; QuickBasket has only 3 → non-compliant. Option A wrongly fixes 'three' as always enough. Option C applies the one-third test that is reserved for a non-executive Chairperson. Option D invents a flat figure of 5. Determinative facts: executive Chairperson + 8-member Board + only 3 IDs.

questions.question: Is QuickBasket's Audit Committee (3 members, 1 independent director, chaired by a non-independent director) compliant with LODR Reg 18?

options.A: Yes — a minimum of three members is enough, regardless of who they are
options.B: No — but only because the committee must have a minimum of five members
options.C: Yes — only a majority of members must be financially literate; independence is not required
options.D: No — the Audit Committee must have at least three members with at least two-thirds being independent directors (here at least 2 of 3), and its chairperson must be an independent director; QuickBasket fails both the two-thirds and the chair requirements

questions.explanation: LODR Reg 18 requires the Audit Committee to have at least three members, with two-thirds being independent directors (so at least 2 of 3 here) and the chairperson being an independent director. QuickBasket has only 1 ID and a non-independent chair — failing both. Option A ignores the independence/chair requirements. Option C substitutes a 'financial literacy' rule for independence. Option B invents a five-member minimum. Determinative facts: 1 ID of 3 (need 2/3) + non-independent chair.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · Nov 2023] Is the ₹950 crore related-party transaction 'material' under LODR Reg 23, requiring prior shareholder approval?

options.A: No — it is material only if it exceeds ₹1,000 crore, and ₹950 crore is below that
options.B: No — materiality is tested at 25% of consolidated turnover, which ₹950 crore does not reach
options.C: Yes — a transaction is material if it exceeds the LOWER of ₹1,000 crore or 10% of consolidated turnover; 10% of ₹9,000 crore = ₹900 crore, which is the lower figure, and ₹950 crore exceeds it, so prior shareholder approval is required and the related party cannot vote
options.D: Yes — but only because it exceeds 5% of turnover, the royalty/brand threshold

questions.explanation: LODR Reg 23 treats an RPT as material if it exceeds the LOWER of ₹1,000 crore OR 10% of consolidated turnover. 10% of ₹9,000 crore = ₹900 crore; the lower of (₹1,000 crore, ₹900 crore) is ₹900 crore, and ₹950 crore exceeds it → material → prior shareholder approval, with the related party barred from voting. Option A applies the HIGHER (₹1,000 crore) figure (the classic trap). Option B uses 25%. Option D uses the 5% royalty/brand threshold (a different test). Determinative figures: lower of ₹1,000 crore and ₹900 crore = ₹900 crore < ₹950 crore.

questions.question: QuickBasket submitted its quarterly financial results on the 50th day after quarter-end. Is this within the LODR timeline?

options.A: Yes — quarterly results may be submitted within 60 days of quarter-end
options.B: No — quarterly financial results must be submitted within 45 days of the end of each quarter; submission on the 50th day is a breach
options.C: Yes — there is no fixed timeline for quarterly results, only for annual results
options.D: No — quarterly results must be submitted within 30 days of quarter-end

questions.explanation: LODR Reg 33 requires quarterly financial results to be submitted within 45 days of the end of the quarter (annual results within 60 days). Submission on the 50th day breaches the 45-day limit. Option A uses the 60-day figure that applies to ANNUAL results (a swap trap). Option C wrongly denies any quarterly timeline. Option D uses 30 days. Determinative figure: day 50 > 45-day limit.

questions.question: QuickBasket is among the top 1,500 listed entities by market capitalisation. Which statement is INCORRECT?

options.A: Being ranked within the top 1,500 (but outside the top 1,000), QuickBasket is automatically required to constitute a Risk Management Committee
options.B: The requirement to constitute a Risk Management Committee under LODR applies to the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation
options.C: A related party who is interested in a material RPT is barred from voting on the resolution approving it
options.D: Quarterly results must be submitted within 45 days and annual results within 60 days

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option A is false: the Risk Management Committee mandate applies to the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation; an entity ranked within the top 1,500 but OUTSIDE the top 1,000 is not automatically caught. Option B correctly states the top-1,000 rule. Option C correctly states the related-party voting bar. Option D correctly states the 45/60-day results timelines. Determinative point: RMC threshold is top 1,000, not top 1,500.

scenarios.scenarioText: Vidya Jyoti Education Society is a charitable society that has been in existence for 4 years and has spent ₹12 lakh on its educational objects over the last three years. It wishes to receive a grant from a foreign philanthropic foundation. Its newsletter is edited by Mr. Joshi. The Society plans to receive the foreign grant into its existing current account at an SBI branch in Pune, and proposes to spend 35% of the foreign contribution on administrative expenses. A sitting member of a State Legislative Assembly sits on the Society's advisory panel and wishes to personally receive a token foreign grant for a separate initiative.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · May 2024] Is Vidya Jyoti eligible for FCRA REGISTRATION to receive the foreign grant?

options.A: Yes — it is more than 3 years old, which is the only requirement
options.B: No — for registration the organisation must be at least 3 years old AND have spent at least ₹15 lakh on its core activities during the preceding three years; having spent only ₹12 lakh, it is ineligible and must instead seek prior permission
options.C: Yes — it has spent more than ₹10 lakh, which satisfies the financial threshold
options.D: No — because it must be at least 5 years old to register

questions.explanation: FCRA registration requires the entity to be at least 3 years old AND to have spent at least ₹15 lakh on its core/aims activities during the preceding three financial years (excluding admin expenditure). Vidya Jyoti spent only ₹12 lakh → ineligible for registration; it may instead apply for prior permission for a specific grant. Option A ignores the spending threshold. Option C uses ₹10 lakh (a related-but-different figure — the FC-receipt intimation level for relatives). Option D uses a 5-year age requirement. Determinative figures: ₹12 lakh spent < ₹15 lakh required.

questions.question: The Society proposes to spend 35% of the foreign contribution on administrative expenses. Is this permissible?

options.A: No — administrative expenses out of foreign contribution cannot exceed 20%; 35% breaches the cap
options.B: Yes — up to 50% of foreign contribution may be used for administrative expenses
options.C: Yes — there is no statutory cap on administrative expenses
options.D: No — the cap is 10%, so 35% is far in excess

questions.explanation: FCRA (Sec 8) caps administrative expenses met out of foreign contribution at 20% (reduced from 50% by the 2020 amendment). 35% exceeds the 20% cap. Option B uses the pre-2020 figure of 50% (the amendment trap). Option C wrongly says no cap. Option D understates the cap as 10%. Determinative figure: 35% > 20% cap.

questions.question: The Society intends to receive the foreign grant into its existing SBI current account in Pune. Is this compliant with FCRA?

options.A: No — foreign contribution must be received only in the designated 'FCRA Account' opened with the State Bank of India, New Delhi Main Branch; a Pune SBI account is not sufficient
