options.B: Yes — any scheduled-bank account may be used to receive foreign contribution
options.C: Yes — any SBI branch account anywhere in India qualifies
options.D: No — but only because the account must be a savings account, not a current account

questions.explanation: Post-2020, FCRA requires foreign contribution to be received only in a designated FCRA account opened with the State Bank of India, New Delhi Main Branch. A Pune SBI account does not meet this requirement (the entity may keep another FCRA-designated bank account for utilisation, but receipt must be in the SBI NDMB account). Option B wrongly allows any scheduled bank. Option C wrongly allows any SBI branch (the specific NDMB requirement is the trap). Option D invents a savings-vs-current distinction. Determinative point: receipt only at SBI New Delhi Main Branch.

questions.question: The sitting Member of the Legislative Assembly on the advisory panel wishes to personally accept a token foreign grant. Which statement is correct under Sec 3?

options.A: He is barred — Sec 3 prohibits specified persons, including legislators (members of a Legislature), from accepting foreign contribution, irrespective of the amount
options.B: He may accept it because the amount is only a token sum
options.C: He may accept it provided he discloses it within 30 days
options.D: He may accept it because the bar applies only to Members of Parliament, not State legislators

questions.explanation: Sec 3 lists categories barred from accepting foreign contribution — including candidates for election, government servants, judges, and members of any Legislature (which includes State Legislative Assembly members), as well as newspaper editors/columnists. The bar is absolute and does not depend on the amount. Option B wrongly relies on the sum being a token. Option C wrongly suggests disclosure cures it. Option D wrongly limits the bar to MPs (legislators of any Legislature are covered). Determinative fact: he is a sitting member of a Legislature.

questions.question: Which statement about Vidya Jyoti's FCRA obligations is INCORRECT?

options.A: An FCRA-registered person cannot transfer foreign contribution to any other person
options.B: The editor of the Society's newsletter, Mr. Joshi, is among the categories barred under Sec 3 from accepting foreign contribution in his own right
options.C: Once registered, the Society may freely transfer a portion of the foreign contribution to any unregistered NGO of its choice
options.D: FCRA registration, once granted, is valid for five years

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option C is false: after the 2020 amendment (Sec 7) an FCRA recipient is prohibited from transferring foreign contribution to ANY other person (registered or not). Option A correctly states that bar. Option B correctly notes that newspaper/newsletter editors are among the Sec 3 barred persons. Option D correctly states the five-year validity of registration. Determinative point: no transfer of foreign contribution to other persons.

scenarios.scenarioText: EverGreen Paper & Packaging Ltd (the holding company) proposes a fast-track merger under Sec 233 with its wholly-owned subsidiary, GreenPack Cartons Ltd. A second proposal contemplates merging EverGreen with an associate, Recyclo Trust (a Section 8 company). For the EverGreen–GreenPack scheme, members representing 92% in number approve it, while creditors representing 88% in value give their consent. A minority group of shareholders, alleging that the scheme conceals a fraudulent diversion, threatens a class action. EverGreen's advisers debate whether the scheme needs NCLT approval or only Regional Director clearance, and how long the Central Government/Regional Director has to raise objections.

questions.question: Can the EverGreen–Recyclo Trust proposal proceed as a fast-track merger under Sec 233, given that Recyclo is a Section 8 company?

options.A: It cannot be undertaken as a fast-track merger on the footing of a Section 8 company being involved unless the conditions are met — the fast-track route is confined to specified classes (e.g. two or more small companies, a holding company and its wholly-owned subsidiary, and certain start-ups), and a Section 8 company does not qualify under the small-company route
options.B: Yes — any two group companies may use Sec 233 regardless of their nature
options.C: Yes — Section 8 companies are expressly the preferred users of Sec 233
options.D: No — because fast-track mergers are available only to listed companies

questions.explanation: Sec 233 is confined to specified classes of companies (two or more small companies; a holding company and its wholly-owned subsidiary; certain start-ups, etc.). A Section 8 company cannot avail the small-company route (a Section 8 company is excluded from the definition of a small company), so the EverGreen–Recyclo proposal does not fit Sec 233. Option B wrongly says 'any group companies'. Option C wrongly favours Section 8 companies. Option D wrongly restricts Sec 233 to listed companies (it is in fact for smaller/specified entities, not listed ones). Determinative fact: Recyclo is a Section 8 company.

questions.question: For the EverGreen–GreenPack fast-track scheme, members approve at 92% in number and creditors consent at 88% in value. Is the approval threshold satisfied?

options.A: Yes — both exceed three-fourths (75%), which is the requirement
options.B: Yes — members at 92% alone are sufficient; creditor consent is not required
options.C: No — Sec 233 requires approval by members holding at least 90% of the total number of shares AND creditors representing at least 9/10ths (90%) in value; members at 92% qualify, but creditors at 88% (below 90%) do not
options.D: No — because members must approve at 9/10ths in VALUE and creditors at 90% in number

questions.explanation: Sec 233(1) requires approval by members holding at least 90% of the total number of shares and by creditors representing at least nine-tenths (90%) in value. Members at 92% (≥90%) qualify, but creditors at 88% fall below the 90% value requirement, so the threshold is not met. Option A uses 75%. Option B wrongly dispenses with creditor consent. Option D swaps the bases (members = number, creditors = value, not the reverse). Determinative figure: creditors 88% < 90% value.

questions.question: Procedurally, where must the EverGreen–GreenPack scheme be filed, and what is the Central Government/Regional Director's window to object?

options.A: It must be sanctioned by the NCLT after a full hearing, like any other merger
options.B: The scheme is filed with the Central Government (Regional Director); if the RD has no objection (or does not communicate an objection) within 60 days, it is registered — there is no NCLT sanction order required for the fast-track route
options.C: It must be filed with the RBI, which has 90 days to object
options.D: It is filed with the Regional Director, who must respond within 30 days, failing which it lapses

questions.explanation: Under Sec 233 the scheme is filed with the Central Government (acting through the Regional Director); if no objection is received within 60 days, the scheme is registered without an NCLT sanction order (the RD may, if it has objections, refer it to the NCLT). Option A wrongly imposes the full NCLT process (that is the Sec 232 route). Option C wrongly routes it to the RBI. Option D uses a 30-day window and a 'lapse' consequence. Determinative point: RD route, 60-day objection window, no NCLT order needed.

questions.question: The minority shareholders allege the scheme conceals fraudulent diversion and threaten a class action under Sec 245. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The eligibility thresholds for a class action can be waived by the Tribunal just as under Sec 244
options.B: A class action lies only against the company, not its directors
options.C: A class action requires only a single aggrieved shareholder and has no threshold
options.D: A class action under Sec 245 may be maintained where the requisite number/percentage of members or depositors join (100 members, or the prescribed percentage, or members holding the prescribed share of issued capital), and these thresholds — unlike Sec 244 — are NOT waivable by the Tribunal

questions.explanation: Sec 245 class actions require the prescribed minimum number of members/depositors (e.g. 100 members, or the prescribed percentage of members, or members holding the prescribed share of issued capital), and these thresholds are NOT waivable (in contrast to Sec 244, where the Tribunal can waive). Option A wrongly imports the Sec 244 waiver. Option C wrongly removes the threshold. Option B wrongly limits respondents (a class action may target directors, auditors, experts and advisers). Determinative point: Sec 245 thresholds are non-waivable.

questions.question: Which statement distinguishing Sec 233 (fast-track) from Sec 232 (Tribunal-route merger) is INCORRECT?

options.A: A Sec 233 fast-track merger does not ordinarily require a Tribunal-convened meeting and sanction order, whereas a Sec 232 merger does
options.B: A Sec 233 merger is confined to specified classes of companies, whereas Sec 232 is generally available
options.C: Under Sec 233, the approval thresholds are 90% of members (by number of shares) and 90% in value of creditors
options.D: A Sec 233 fast-track merger requires the same 3/4-in-value approval at a Tribunal-convened class meeting as a Sec 232 scheme

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option D is false: the fast-track route uses the 90% members (by number of shares) / 90% creditors-in-value consent route, NOT a Tribunal-convened meeting with the 3/4-in-value approval that characterises Sec 230/232. Options A, B and C correctly state the distinctions. Determinative point: Sec 233 uses 90%/90% consents, not the Sec 230 3/4-in-value meeting.

scenarios.scenarioText: StridePro Footwear Ltd plans an IPO. In each of the last three financial years it had net tangible assets of ₹4 crore, but in the most recent year 60% of those assets were held in monetary form. Its average pre-tax operating profit over three of the preceding five years works out to ₹14 crore. Its net worth was ₹1.2 crore in each of the three preceding years. The merchant bankers propose a minimum promoters' contribution that will be locked in, and set an IPO price band with a floor of ₹100 and a cap of ₹125. The promoters also hold shares in excess of the minimum contribution that they intend to offer for sale.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · Nov 2023] Does StridePro meet the profitability condition for an IPO under the ICDR 'eligibility (profitability) route', given an average pre-tax operating profit of ₹14 crore?

options.A: Yes — an average pre-tax operating profit of ₹10 crore is enough, which it exceeds
options.B: No — the route requires an average pre-tax operating profit of at least ₹15 crore in at least three of the preceding five years; ₹14 crore falls short, so StridePro must take the alternative book-built (QIB) route
options.C: Yes — ₹14 crore comfortably exceeds the ₹3 crore requirement
options.D: No — the requirement is ₹25 crore of operating profit, which it does not meet

questions.explanation: The ICDR profitability route requires (among other conditions) an average pre-tax operating profit of at least ₹15 crore in at least three of the immediately preceding five years. StridePro's ₹14 crore falls short, so it cannot use the profitability route and must instead make the issue through the book-built route allocating to QIBs. Option A uses ₹10 crore. Option C confuses this with the ₹3 crore net-tangible-asset condition. Option D uses ₹25 crore. Determinative figure: ₹14 crore < ₹15 crore.

questions.question: StridePro had net tangible assets of ₹4 crore in each of the three years, but 60% were monetary in the most recent year. Does it satisfy the net-tangible-assets condition?

options.A: No — although the ₹3 crore minimum is met, the condition also requires that not more than 50% of the net tangible assets be held in monetary assets; with 60% in monetary form, it fails
options.B: Yes — ₹4 crore exceeds the ₹3 crore minimum, so the condition is fully met
options.C: Yes — there is no restriction on the composition of net tangible assets
options.D: No — because net tangible assets must be at least ₹10 crore each year

questions.explanation: The net-tangible-assets condition requires NTA of at least ₹3 crore in each of the three preceding years, of which NOT MORE THAN 50% may be held in monetary assets (a higher 50%+ monetary holding is allowed only if firm commitments to deploy have been made in the offer document). StridePro meets the ₹3 crore floor (₹4 crore) but 60% is in monetary assets, breaching the 50% cap. Option B ignores the monetary-asset composition condition. Option C wrongly says there is no composition restriction. Option D uses ₹10 crore. Determinative figure: 60% monetary > 50% cap.

questions.question: What is the minimum promoters' contribution lock-in position under the ICDR Regulations?

options.A: The minimum promoters' contribution is 20% of the post-issue capital, locked in for 3 years from the date of allotment
options.B: The minimum promoters' contribution is 25% of the pre-issue capital, locked in for 1 year
options.C: The minimum promoters' contribution is 20% of the post-issue capital, locked in for 18 months from the date of allotment
options.D: The minimum promoters' contribution is 10% of the post-issue capital, locked in for 6 months

questions.explanation: Under the amended ICDR Regulations, the minimum promoters' contribution (20% of the post-issue capital) is locked in for 18 months from the date of allotment (reduced from the earlier 3 years). Option A uses the PRE-amendment 3-year lock-in (the amendment trap). Option B misstates both the base (pre-issue) and percentage. Option D uses the 6-month figure (which applies to promoters' holding in EXCESS of the minimum contribution, not the minimum itself). Determinative point: 20% of post-issue capital, 18-month lock-in.

questions.question: The merchant bankers set a price band with a floor of ₹100 and a cap of ₹125. Is this price band permissible under the ICDR Regulations?

options.A: Yes — the cap may be up to the floor price plus ₹120, so ₹125 is well within range
options.B: Yes — there is no relationship prescribed between the floor and the cap
options.C: No — the cap of the price band cannot be more than 120% of the floor price; 120% of ₹100 = ₹120, so a cap of ₹125 is impermissible
options.D: No — the cap cannot exceed 150% of the floor, so ₹125 is invalid only marginally

questions.explanation: ICDR provides that the cap of the price band shall not be more than 120% of the floor price — a MULTIPLICATIVE relationship. 120% of ₹100 = ₹120; a cap of ₹125 exceeds it and is impermissible. Option A treats it as additive (floor + ₹120 = ₹220), a classic misreading. Option B wrongly denies any relationship. Option D uses 150%. Determinative figures: cap ₹125 > 120% × ₹100 = ₹120.

questions.question: Which statement regarding StridePro's IPO is INCORRECT?

options.A: If StridePro cannot meet the profitability route, it may still make an IPO through the book-built route with allocation to qualified institutional buyers
options.B: Promoters' holdings in excess of the minimum contribution are locked in for a shorter period than the minimum contribution itself
options.C: The cap of the price band is capped at 120% of the floor price
options.D: Because its net tangible assets are ₹4 crore, StridePro satisfies the eligibility condition regardless of how those assets are composed

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option D is false: meeting the ₹3 crore NTA floor is not enough — not more than 50% may be in monetary assets, and StridePro's 60% monetary holding breaches that, so composition does matter. Option A correctly states the alternative QIB/book-built route. Option B correctly notes the shorter (6-month) lock-in for excess promoter holding. Option C correctly states the 120% price-band cap. Determinative point: NTA composition (monetary-asset cap) matters.

scenarios.scenarioText: Imperial Ceramics PLC is a company incorporated in the United Kingdom. On 1 March 2026 it establishes a branch office in Mumbai to sell tiles in India, marking its first place of business in India. Sixty per cent of Imperial's paid-up share capital is held by Indian citizens and Indian companies. Imperial delays filing the prescribed particulars of its Indian establishment and certain documents with the Registrar. Separately, in connection with an Indian securities matter, Imperial fails to furnish information called for by SEBI for 40 days. A more serious allegation of a deliberate, fraudulent securities-market contravention by Imperial is also being examined for possible criminal prosecution.

questions.question: Given that 60% of Imperial's paid-up capital is held by Indian citizens/companies, what is the consequence under Sec 379?

options.A: None — a foreign company is never subject to Indian company-law provisions beyond basic registration
options.B: Where not less than 50% of the paid-up share capital of a foreign company is held by Indian citizens/companies, the foreign company must comply with the provisions of Chapter XXII (and such other provisions as prescribed) as if it were an Indian company in respect of its Indian business
options.C: It applies only if 75% or more is held by Indian citizens/companies
options.D: It applies only if the foreign company is listed in India

questions.explanation: Sec 379(2) provides that where not less than 50% of the paid-up capital (equity or preference, or partly each) of a foreign company is held by Indian citizens and/or Indian companies, the foreign company must comply with Chapter XXII provisions (and prescribed provisions) as if it were a company incorporated in India, in respect of its Indian business. Imperial's 60% Indian holding crosses 50%, so the provision applies. Option A wrongly exempts foreign companies. Option C uses a 75% threshold. Option D adds a listing condition. Determinative figure: 60% ≥ 50%.

questions.question: Within what time must Imperial deliver the prescribed particulars/documents to the Registrar after establishing its place of business in India under Sec 380?

options.A: Within 60 days of establishing the place of business
options.B: Within 30 days of the establishment of the place of business in India
options.C: Within 90 days of establishing the place of business
options.D: Within 6 months of establishing the place of business

questions.explanation: Sec 380 requires a foreign company, within 30 days of establishing a place of business in India, to deliver to the Registrar the prescribed documents/particulars (charter, registered/principal office, directors/secretary, authorised representative in India, etc.). Option A uses 60 days. Option C uses 90 days. Option D uses 6 months. Determinative point: 30-day filing window under Sec 380.

questions.question: Imperial has delayed its filings with the Registrar. Which statement about late filing of documents (Chapter on e-filing) is correct?

options.A: Late filings are simply rejected; there is no mechanism to file them late
options.B: There is no consequence whatsoever for late filing of documents with the Registrar
options.C: Late filings attract only imprisonment, never a monetary fee
options.D: A document required to be filed may be filed after the prescribed time on payment of such additional fee (and higher additional fee for repeated defaults) as prescribed, in addition to the normal fee

questions.explanation: Sec 403 (read with the e-filing provisions) permits filing of documents after the prescribed period on payment of additional fees (with higher additional fees for repeated defaults), in addition to the normal fee, without prejudice to other liability. Option A wrongly says late filing is impossible. Option C wrongly says only imprisonment. Option B wrongly says no consequence. Determinative point: additional fee mechanism for late filing.

questions.question: Imperial fails to furnish information called for by SEBI for 40 days. What is the maximum penalty under Sec 15A of the SEBI Act for this failure to furnish information?

options.A: A flat ₹1 crore regardless of the number of days
options.B: ₹1 lakh for each day during which the failure continues, subject to a maximum of ₹1 crore — so for 40 days the penalty is ₹40 lakh (within the ₹1 crore cap)
options.C: The higher of ₹25 crore or three times any gain
options.D: ₹1 lakh in total, irrespective of the duration

questions.explanation: Sec 15A penalises failure to furnish information/returns/documents at ₹1 lakh for each day of continuing failure, subject to a maximum of ₹1 crore. For 40 days that is ₹40 lakh (40 × ₹1 lakh), within the ₹1 crore cap. Option A treats ₹1 crore as a flat penalty. Option C uses the Sec 15G/15HA insider/fraud formula (higher of ₹25 crore or 3× gain — a cross-provision trap). Option D treats ₹1 lakh as a one-time figure. Determinative figures: 40 days × ₹1 lakh = ₹40 lakh, under the ₹1 crore cap.

questions.question: For the alleged deliberate fraudulent securities contravention, which statement about criminal prosecution under Sec 24 of the SEBI Act is INCORRECT?

options.A: Contravention of the SEBI Act/regulations can attract imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years, or fine up to ₹25 crore, or both
options.B: Criminal prosecution under Sec 24 is independent of monetary penalties imposed by an adjudicating officer
options.C: The maximum imprisonment under Sec 24 is capped at 6 months in every case
options.D: A fine under Sec 24 can be as high as ₹25 crore

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option C is false: Sec 24(1) provides for imprisonment up to 10 years (not a 6-month cap) and/or a fine up to ₹25 crore. Option A correctly states the 10-year/₹25 crore range. Option B correctly states that criminal prosecution is independent of adjudication penalties. Option D correctly states the ₹25 crore fine ceiling. Determinative point: Sec 24 imprisonment can extend to 10 years, not 6 months.

scenarios.scenarioText: CONCEPT-BASED SET (no fact scenario): integrated, cross-chapter questions on numbers that recur with DIFFERENT meanings across Corporate & Economic Laws (the cross-law traps). Choose the option that correctly maps the number to its law and meaning.

questions.question: The figure '182 days' appears in both the Companies Act (resident director) and FEMA (person resident in India). Which statement correctly distinguishes them?

options.A: Both compute the 182 days on a financial-year (April–March) basis
options.B: The Companies Act resident-director test counts 182 days in the CALENDAR year, whereas FEMA counts more than 182 days in the preceding FINANCIAL year (April–March)
options.C: Both compute the 182 days on a calendar-year basis
options.D: The Companies Act uses the financial year and FEMA uses the calendar year

questions.explanation: Sec 149(3) (resident director) requires stay in India for at least 182 days during the CALENDAR/financial year as specified for that purpose (the resident-director computation is tied to the calendar year), while FEMA Sec 2(v) uses MORE than 182 days in the preceding FINANCIAL year (April–March). Option D reverses them; Options A and C wrongly make both the same. This is the classic same-number/different-window trap.

questions.question: The amount '₹1 crore' and '₹1 lakh' collide across the IBC and the Companies Act. Which mapping is correct?

options.A: ₹1 crore is the minimum default threshold to initiate CIRP under the IBC (raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020), whereas ₹1 lakh is the demand figure for 'inability to pay debts' under the Companies Act winding-up provisions
options.B: ₹1 lakh is the current IBC default threshold; ₹1 crore is the Companies Act inability-to-pay demand figure
options.C: Both the IBC threshold and the Companies Act demand figure are ₹1 crore
options.D: Both are ₹1 lakh

questions.explanation: The IBC minimum default to trigger CIRP is ₹1 crore (raised from ₹1 lakh by the March 2020 notification). The Companies Act 'inability to pay debts' demand figure (for a creditor's winding-up petition) remains a sum exceeding ₹1 lakh. Option B reverses the two. Options C and D wrongly equate them. The trap: applying ₹1 crore to a Companies Act winding-up demand, or the old ₹1 lakh to the IBC.

questions.question: Which statement about the '66%' and '75%' voting thresholds is correct?

options.A: Approval of a resolution plan (and key CoC decisions) under the IBC requires 66% of the voting share — reduced from the 75% that applied before the 2018/2019 amendments
options.B: A resolution plan and routine CoC decisions under the IBC require 75% of the voting share
options.C: The IBC CoC threshold is 50% for all decisions
options.D: The IBC requires 90% CoC approval for a resolution plan

questions.explanation: Post-amendment, the IBC requires 66% of the CoC voting share to approve a resolution plan and other significant decisions (certain routine matters need a simple 51% majority). The 75% figure is the PRE-amendment threshold (the trap), and also echoes the Sec 230 3/4-in-value compromise threshold. Option B uses the old 75%. Option C uses 51% across the board. Option D uses 90% (a Sec 230(9)/Sec 233 figure).

questions.question: The figure '90%' appears in several Companies Act provisions but on DIFFERENT bases (number vs value). Which statement is correct?

options.A: Sec 230(9) dispensation needs 90% in VALUE (by affidavit), whereas Sec 233 fast-track member approval needs members holding 90% of the total NUMBER of shares — different bases, same percentage
options.B: Sec 230(9) meeting-dispensation and Sec 233 fast-track member approval are both measured in NUMBER of members
options.C: Both Sec 230(9) and Sec 233 use 90% in value of creditors only
options.D: Sec 233 requires 90% of creditors in NUMBER and 90% of members in VALUE

questions.explanation: Sec 230(9) allows dispensation of a creditors' meeting where creditors representing 90% in VALUE agree by affidavit; Sec 233 fast-track requires approval by members holding 90% of the total NUMBER of shares (and creditors representing 90% in value). The trap is mixing the number/value bases. Option B wrongly makes both 'number'. Option C and D misstate the bases.

questions.question: Which statement about the '5%' and '10%' thresholds across the laws is INCORRECT?

options.A: Under SAST, an acquirer in the 25%-75% band may creep up to 5% of voting rights per financial year without an open offer
options.B: Under Sec 230(4), creditors holding at least 5% of outstanding debt and shareholders holding at least 10% of shareholding may object to a scheme
options.C: Under Sec 244, the shareholding-based eligibility for an oppression petition is 5% of the issued capital
options.D: Under SAST/PIT, initial disclosure of shareholding is triggered on crossing 5% of shares/voting rights

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option C is false: the Sec 244 shareholding-based eligibility is one-TENTH (10%) of issued capital (the 5% issued-capital figure is the THIRD alternative under the Sec 245 class-action route, not Sec 244). Option A correctly states SAST creeping (5%/FY). Option B correctly states the Sec 230(4) objection thresholds (5% debt / 10% shareholding). Option D correctly states the 5% initial-disclosure trigger.

scenarios.scenarioText: CONCEPT-BASED SET (no fact scenario): integrated questions on eligibility, waivers, ineligibility and remuneration limits across the Companies Act and the IBC. Choose the option that states the law correctly.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts the WAIVER position under Sec 244 (oppression) and Sec 245 (class action)?

options.A: Both Sec 244 and Sec 245 eligibility thresholds can be waived by the Tribunal
options.B: The Sec 245 thresholds can be waived, but the Sec 244 thresholds cannot
options.C: Neither Sec 244 nor Sec 245 thresholds can be waived under any circumstances
options.D: The Tribunal may waive the Sec 244 eligibility thresholds, but the Sec 245 class-action thresholds cannot be waived

questions.explanation: The proviso to Sec 244(1) gives the Tribunal a discretion to waive the eligibility requirements for an oppression/mismanagement petition; Sec 245 contains no such waiver power, so its thresholds are firm. Option B reverses the rule. Options A and C wrongly equate the two. The trap: assuming the class-action thresholds are equally relaxable.

questions.question: Under Sec 165, the limits on the number of directorships a person may hold are:

options.A: A maximum of 20 companies in all, of which the number of PUBLIC companies cannot exceed 10
options.B: A maximum of 15 companies in all, of which up to 10 may be public companies
options.C: A maximum of 20 public companies, with no overall limit
options.D: A maximum of 10 companies in all, of which up to 5 may be public companies

questions.explanation: Sec 165 caps the total number of directorships at 20, with a sub-limit that the number of PUBLIC companies must not exceed 10 (for the public-company sub-limit, private companies that are holding/subsidiaries of public companies are counted). Option B uses 15 (the maximum number of directors a company may have under Sec 149 before a special resolution — a cross-provision trap). Option C drops the overall cap. Option D halves both figures.

questions.question: Which of the following persons is NOT, by reason of the matters stated, rendered ineligible to submit a resolution plan under Sec 29A of the IBC?

options.A: An undischarged insolvent
options.B: A person whose account is classified as a non-performing asset for one year or more and who has not cleared the overdue amounts
options.C: A financial creditor who is a scheduled bank acquiring the debt in the ordinary course, with no disqualifying attribute
options.D: A person who is a wilful defaulter

questions.explanation: Sec 29A lists disqualifying attributes — undischarged insolvent (A), NPA for one year or more without clearing dues (B), wilful defaulter (D), connected persons, certain convicts, and guarantors whose guarantee is invoked. A scheduled bank/financial creditor with no disqualifying attribute is not, merely by being a creditor, ineligible. Option C is therefore the correct answer (the person NOT rendered ineligible). The trap: assuming any creditor or any prior connection automatically disqualifies.

questions.question: In a loss/inadequate-profit year, which Schedule V Part II base limit on managerial remuneration is correctly stated?

options.A: Effective capital of ₹5 crore to less than ₹100 crore → base limit ₹84 lakh (which may be doubled by special resolution)
options.B: Effective capital of ₹5 crore to less than ₹100 crore → base limit ₹60 lakh
options.C: Effective capital of ₹100 crore to less than ₹250 crore → base limit ₹84 lakh
options.D: Effective capital below ₹5 crore → base limit ₹120 lakh

questions.explanation: Under the current Schedule V Part II slabs, effective capital of ₹5 crore to less than ₹100 crore carries a base yearly limit of ₹84 lakh (doubled to ₹168 lakh by special resolution). Option B uses the pre-amendment ₹60 lakh for that slab. Option C mismatches the ₹100-250 crore slab (which is ₹120 lakh) with ₹84 lakh. Option D assigns ₹120 lakh to the lowest slab (it is ₹60 lakh). The trap: pre-amendment figures and adjacent-slab swaps.

questions.question: Which statement on forum and jurisdiction is INCORRECT?

options.A: An appeal from an order of the NCLT lies to the NCLAT
options.B: An appeal from an order of the NCLAT lies to the Supreme Court only on a question of law
options.C: A civil court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit in respect of any matter which the NCLT or NCLAT is empowered to determine
options.D: The NCLT may, in oppression/mismanagement proceedings, order the winding up of a company as a remedy

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option C is false: Sec 430 bars civil courts from entertaining suits/proceedings in respect of matters the NCLT/NCLAT is empowered to determine. Option A correctly states the NCLT→NCLAT appeal. Option B correctly states the question-of-law-only appeal to the Supreme Court (Sec 423). Option D correctly states that winding up is available as a Sec 242 remedy.

scenarios.scenarioText: CONCEPT-BASED SET (no fact scenario): integrated questions on statutory timelines and outer limits across the Companies Act, the IBC and SEBI SAST/LODR. Choose the option that states the timeline correctly.

questions.question: What is the limitation (and maximum condonable) period for an appeal from the NCLT to the NCLAT?

options.A: 30 days, with a further 30 days condonable (60 days maximum)
options.B: 60 days, with no condonation
options.C: 45 days, with a further 45 days condonable on sufficient cause (90 days maximum)
options.D: 90 days, with a further 90 days condonable (180 days maximum)

questions.explanation: Sec 421(3) gives 45 days to appeal to the NCLAT, with a proviso allowing condonation of a further period not exceeding 45 days on sufficient cause — an outer limit of 90 days. Option A uses 30+30. Option B denies condonation. Option D doubles the figures. The trap: the commonly-confused 30-day or 60-day appeal periods.

questions.question: Under the SAST Regulations, within what time must the public announcement of an open offer ordinarily be made on triggering the obligation?

options.A: Within 2 working days of the trigger
options.B: Within 15 working days of the trigger
options.C: Within 7 calendar days of the trigger
options.D: Within 4 working days of entering into the agreement/triggering the obligation

questions.explanation: SAST Reg 13(1) requires the public announcement to be made on the date of agreeing to acquire (or triggering the obligation) — generally within 4 working days for relevant triggers. Option A uses 2 days (the disclosure-filing timeline, a cross-trap). Option C and B use 7 and 15 days. The trap: confusing the 4-working-day PA timeline with the 2-working-day disclosure timeline.

questions.question: Under LODR, the timelines for submitting financial results are:

options.A: Quarterly within 60 days; annual within 45 days
options.B: Both quarterly and annual within 45 days
options.C: Quarterly within 30 days; annual within 90 days
options.D: Quarterly within 45 days of quarter-end; annual within 60 days of year-end

questions.explanation: LODR Reg 33 requires quarterly results within 45 days of the end of each quarter and annual (audited) results within 60 days of the end of the financial year. Option A reverses the two (the classic swap trap). Option C uses 30/90. Option B wrongly makes both 45.

questions.question: What is the timeline for completion of the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) under the IBC?

options.A: 180 days, extendable by 90 days (270 days), with an overall outer limit of 330 days including time taken in legal proceedings
options.B: 270 days, extendable by 90 days (360 days), with no outer limit
options.C: 180 days, with no extension permitted
options.D: 330 days, extendable by a further 90 days (420 days)

questions.explanation: CIRP must ordinarily be completed within 180 days, extendable once by up to 90 days (270 days), subject to an overall outer limit of 330 days, INCLUDING any time spent in legal proceedings (Sec 12 as amended). Option B misstates the base and removes the outer limit. Option C denies the extension. Option D inflates the outer limit. The trap: forgetting the 330-day cap that subsumes litigation time.

questions.question: Which statement on Companies Act timelines is INCORRECT?

options.A: There must not be a gap of more than 120 days between two consecutive Board meetings
options.B: A company must hold its first Board meeting within 30 days of the date of its incorporation
options.C: A foreign company must deliver the prescribed documents to the Registrar within 30 days of establishing a place of business in India
options.D: Notice of a Board meeting must ordinarily be given at least 21 days in advance

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option D is false: notice of a BOARD meeting is at least 7 days (the 21-day notice is for a GENERAL meeting — a cross-provision trap). Option A correctly states the 120-day maximum gap (Sec 173). Option B correctly states the 30-day first-board-meeting rule. Option C correctly states the Sec 380 30-day foreign-company filing.

scenarios.scenarioText: CONCEPT-BASED SET (no fact scenario): integrated questions on penalties and consequences across the SEBI Act, FEMA, the IBC, the Companies Act and FCRA. Choose the option that states the consequence correctly.

questions.question: Which mapping of SEBI Act penalty provisions is correct?

options.A: Sec 15A (failure to furnish information): higher of ₹25 crore or 3× the gain
options.B: Sec 15A: ₹1 lakh per day of default, subject to a maximum of ₹1 crore; Sec 15G (insider trading): higher of ₹25 crore or 3× the profit made
options.C: Sec 15G: ₹1 lakh per day, capped at ₹1 crore; Sec 15A: higher of ₹25 crore or 3× profit
options.D: Both Sec 15A and Sec 15G carry a flat ₹1 crore penalty

questions.explanation: Sec 15A penalises failure to furnish information at ₹1 lakh per day, subject to a ₹1 crore maximum; Sec 15G penalises insider trading at the higher of ₹25 crore or three times the profit. Option A wrongly applies the insider-trading formula to Sec 15A. Option C reverses the two provisions. Option D wrongly flattens both to ₹1 crore. The trap: swapping the per-day-capped penalty with the higher-of-₹25-crore-or-3× formula.

questions.question: Under Sec 13 of FEMA, which statement on penalties is correct?

options.A: Where the amount is quantifiable, the penalty may extend to up to three times the sum involved; where it is not quantifiable, up to ₹2 lakh; and for continuing contraventions, a further penalty up to ₹5,000 per day
options.B: Where the amount is quantifiable, the penalty is a flat ₹2 lakh
options.C: All FEMA contraventions carry imprisonment up to 5 years
options.D: The penalty is always 3× the sum, whether or not the amount is quantifiable

questions.explanation: Sec 13(1) provides: where the contravention amount is quantifiable, penalty up to three times that sum; where not quantifiable, up to ₹2 lakh; and where the contravention continues, a further penalty up to ₹5,000 for every day of continuance. Option B wrongly applies the flat ₹2 lakh to a quantifiable amount. Option C wrongly says imprisonment (FEMA is primarily a civil/penalty regime). Option D wrongly applies 3× even where the amount is not quantifiable.

questions.question: Under the Sec 53 IBC liquidation waterfall, which order of priority is correct (highest first)?

options.A: Secured creditors → CIRP/liquidation costs → workmen's dues → Government dues → equity shareholders
options.B: Government dues → CIRP costs → secured creditors → workmen → equity shareholders
options.C: CIRP and liquidation costs → (workmen's dues for 24 months + secured creditors who relinquished security, pari passu) → wages/employee dues for 12 months → unsecured financial creditors → Government dues and remaining secured debt → preference shareholders → equity shareholders
options.D: Equity shareholders → preference shareholders → unsecured creditors → secured creditors → CIRP costs

questions.explanation: Sec 53 ranks: (1) insolvency resolution/liquidation costs; (2) workmen's dues for 24 months and secured creditors (who relinquished security) pari passu; (3) wages/employee dues for 12 months; (4) unsecured financial creditors; (5) Government dues and remaining secured debt; (6) preference shareholders; (7) equity shareholders. Option A wrongly puts secured creditors ahead of CIRP costs. Option B elevates Government dues. Option D inverts the entire order. The trap: misplacing CIRP costs or the workmen-24m/employee-12m periods.

questions.question: Which statement on director disqualification and vacation of office is INCORRECT?

options.A: A conviction with a sentence of imprisonment of not less than 6 months disqualifies a person, with the disqualification continuing for 5 years from expiry of the sentence
options.B: A conviction with a sentence of 7 years or more results in permanent disqualification
options.C: On incurring a Sec 164(2) disqualification (e.g. the company's 3-year non-filing), a director vacates office in the defaulting company itself but continues on all other boards
options.D: A disqualification under Sec 164(2) extends to appointment/reappointment in other companies as well

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option C reverses the Sec 167(1)(a) proviso: a director who incurs a Sec 164(2) disqualification vacates office in all OTHER companies but continues in the DEFAULTING company (so as to remain accountable). Option A correctly states the 6-month/5-year rule. Option B correctly states the 7-year permanent bar. Option D correctly states that the disqualification reaches other companies. The trap: flipping which company the director continues in.

questions.question: Which statement on FCRA consequences and conditions is INCORRECT?

options.A: Administrative expenses met out of foreign contribution cannot exceed 20% of such contribution
options.B: An FCRA-registered person may freely transfer foreign contribution to other persons who are not registered under the FCRA
options.C: Foreign contribution must be received only in the designated FCRA account with the State Bank of India, New Delhi Main Branch
options.D: For registration, an organisation must normally be at least 3 years old and have spent at least ₹15 lakh on its core activities in the preceding three years

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Option B is false: after the 2020 amendment (Sec 7) a recipient of foreign contribution cannot transfer it to ANY other person (whether or not registered). Option A correctly states the 20% administrative-expense cap. Option C correctly states the SBI New Delhi Main Branch designated-account requirement. Option D correctly states the registration eligibility (3 years old + ₹15 lakh spent). The trap: assuming onward transfer to other registered/unregistered NGOs is permitted.
